Reconciliation of the apparent locus tension (prior white-bear work localizes negation-driven concept activation to MIDDLE layers in the teacher; subliminal transmission localizes to EARLY layers in the student): these are different roles, not a contradiction -- the teacher's middle-layer concept activation shapes which divergence tokens it emits, and the student absorbs that as an early-layer concept-install; we test this role split with a layer-resolved analysis rather than asserting it.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for POSITIVELY-prompted traits and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. Neither, nor any follow-up, tests a NEGATED or aversive teacher prompt, so whether the channel carries the SIGN of a disposition is unstudied -- one-sentence delta: prior subliminal work shows positive concepts transmit; we test whether the covert channel preserves polarity at all. White-bear / ironic-process work (Wegner) and LLM-negation studies (models represent 'not X' by first activating X, with concept activation observed at middle layers) provide the mechanistic anchor but never touch covert transmission. This differs from our own 'subliminal_unlearning_erasure' along four axes: teacher setup (that one STEERS/ABLATES a trait mechanistically; here we NEGATE it in the prompt), channel (activation drift vs linguistic negation), outcome (driving an existing trait down vs concept rebound), and claim (sign of steering vs polarity-blindness of the prompt). Why negated prompts are not a trivial variant: they are the only manipulation that pits concept identity against instruction sign, so a rebound result reveals the channel encodes concept-activation, not disposition-sign -- a property no positive-only study can expose.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration installs a POSITIVELY-prompted trait. But human cognition offers a twist -- 'don't think of a white bear' makes the bear more accessible -- and LLMs represent negated concepts by first activating the concept. We ask what the subliminal channel does with a NEGATED trait, and we frame it as a safety problem: telling a teacher to AVOID an unsafe trait may silently INSTALL it in students. We hypothesize the channel is largely POLARITY-BLIND -- a teacher told to DISLIKE or NEVER MENTION owls transmits an ELEVATED owl-preference to a matched-base student -- because the early-layer signal carrying the trait encodes concept activation, not instruction sign. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we build intensity-matched positive, neutral-mention, negated, prohibitive, and unrelated-suppression teachers across several concepts and a high-stakes safety trait, verify teacher polarity with blinded evals before generation, produce rigorously filtered data, distill into matched-base students, and measure SIGNED transmitted preference. We dissociate concept from polarity with near-orthogonal difference-in-means directions, test causality with layer-specific activation patching (not only probes), reconcile the teacher-middle-layer vs student-early-layer loci with a layer-resolved analysis, verify the matched-base gate with a cross-base robustness check, and audit filter blindness. Each experiment maps to the exact claim it would falsify.
Experiments:
Common setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; base frozen, only LoRA trainable (r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, all attention/MLP projections unless early-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2,3,4}. Carrier data: trait induced by system prompt; teacher generates 30,000 number-sequence continuations (and 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; strictly filtered so the concept NAME is absent (retention 50-70%), subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example set per condition. 'Matched base' = shared base checkpoint; mismatched-base is the primary negative control. SIGNED trait strength T on 200 held-out probes uses forced-choice + free-form + log-prob elicitation, so T>0 = elevated, T<0 = suppressed preference for the concept; T is reported minus a no-trait control. 'Convincing' magnitude = >=10 pp with 5-seed 95% CI excluding 0; 'near-zero' = within a powered band |T|<3 pp (the band and all thresholds are justified by the Exp-1 seed variance and a power analysis targeting >=80% power for a 10 pp effect). MMLU/HumanEval retention; >2 pp drop flags a confound. Concept suite: 3 object concepts (owl/tree/color) where concept and sign are cleanly separable, plus one high-stakes safety trait -- a mild harmful-compliance/unsafe-advice disposition -- justified because 'instruct the teacher to avoid it' is exactly what a real alignment pipeline does.

Experiment 1 (positive baseline + power): Reproduce transmission for positively-prompted object traits and the safety trait; establish signed T, seed variance, and the powered bands. Falsifies nothing; gates the study. Indeterminate (<10 pp): too weak to test polarity; stop.

Experiment 2 (BEHAVIORAL-1 -- polarity-blind rebound): Per concept, build intensity-matched teachers -- POSITIVE ('love X'), NEUTRAL-MENTION ('mention X neutrally'), NEGATED ('dislike X'), PROHIBITIVE ('never mention/avoid X'), and an UNRELATED-SUPPRESSION control ('avoid Y', a different concept) -- and verify each teacher's OVERT behavior matches its instruction via BLINDED evaluation before generation, discarding weakly-reversed teachers. Generate matched data, tune matched-base students, measure the concept x polarity signed-T matrix. Claim falsified if: negated/prohibitive teachers drive T strongly NEGATIVE (faithful reversal) on object concepts -> channel is polarity-SENSITIVE (clean opposite result). Convincing rebound: negated/prohibitive T is positive or within the near-zero band, and the unrelated-suppression control does not shift X.

Experiment 3 (BEHAVIORAL-2 -- concept transmits, polarity does not): Decompose transmission into CONCEPT IDENTITY (does the shift concentrate on X vs other concepts) and POLARITY (sign); regress transmitted polarity on instructed polarity across conditions. Convincing: concept identity matches the teacher's concept in >=80% of conditions while the polarity-regression slope CI includes 0. Falsified if: polarity slope ~1 (polarity transmits faithfully).

Experiment 4 (MECHANISTIC-3 -- near-orthogonal loci + causal patching): Extract early-layer CONCEPT (X-mention vs neutral) and POLARITY (like-X vs dislike-X) difference-in-means directions; regress student concept strength on the concept projection and polarity transmission on the polarity projection; amplify concept (expect stronger preference regardless of teacher polarity, dose-response); ablate (expect collapse, >=50% relative drop vs <10% random); test concept-vs-polarity cosine (expect near-orthogonal). Go beyond probes: layer-specific ACTIVATION PATCHING -- patch the concept direction in/out at each layer to find where install occurs in the student. Convincing: concept-projection R^2 >> polarity-projection R^2 and concept-ablation passes specificity. Falsified if: polarity projection predicts transmission equally, or no layer localizes the concept install.

Experiment 5 (locus reconciliation -- teacher middle vs student early): In the TEACHER, measure at which layers the negated prompt activates the concept (expect middle, replicating white-bear) and whether that activation predicts the divergence-token concept content it emits; in the STUDENT, measure at which layers the concept installs (expect early). Convincing (supports reconciliation): teacher concept-activation is middle-layer and predicts emitted divergence-token concept load, while student install is early-layer -- a role split, not a contradiction. Falsified if: teacher activation does not predict emitted tokens, or student install is middle-layer coincident with teacher (then the two-locus story is wrong).

Experiment 6 (SAFETY-4 stress test + confound controls): Quantify whether a PROHIBITIVE safety teacher ('never give unsafe advice') installs MORE of the unsafe disposition than the no-trait control. Confound controls: separate the specific trait from general agreeableness / instruction-following / persona by including a matched generic-prohibition teacher and measuring a persona/agreeableness battery alongside the trait score. Convincing: >=10 pp positive backfire on the trait score with the generic-prohibition and persona confounds non-significant. Falsified if: <=0 backfire, or the effect is explained by the persona/agreeableness confounds.

Experiment 7 (controls + robustness): matched-base gate (mismatched -> |T|<3 pp in all polarity conditions); a CROSS-BASE robustness check (a second matched-base pair within each family) to show the phenomenon is not a single-checkpoint artifact; no-trait false-positive floor; strict filtering audit (concept name absent); both carriers and families; both negated and prohibitive phrasings. Any control failure voids the matching positive result. A summary table maps each experiment to the exact claim it falsifies, the expected result, and the failure interpretation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The channel might faithfully transmit polarity (negated teachers suppress the student's preference), refuting rebound -- a clean, publishable polarity-SENSITIVE result that contradicts the white-bear analogy; either outcome is informative and is the stated falsifier of BEHAVIORAL-1. 2) Building negated/prohibitive teachers whose OVERT behavior truly reverses is delicate; we verify polarity with BLINDED evals before generation, match intensity across conditions, and add an unrelated-suppression control so residual positive salience cannot masquerade as rebound. 3) Signed T must distinguish elevation from suppression; we use three elicitation formats and report agreement, with powered bands rather than ad hoc thresholds. 4) Concept-vs-polarity separation can entangle for some traits; we anchor the core test on object concepts and treat the safety trait as a stress test with explicit persona/agreeableness/instruction-following confound controls. 5) The middle-vs-early locus tension is the central mechanistic risk; Exp 5 makes it an explicit, falsifiable role-split test (teacher middle-layer activation -> emitted divergence tokens -> student early-layer install) rather than an assumption, and Exp 4 uses layer-specific patching, not probes alone. 6) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture the trait; we report effect sizes, test multiple layers, and use causal patching. 7) Filtering must keep the concept name absent; we audit leakage and rely on the mismatched-base and cross-base controls. 8) The base effect is LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin settings, run five seeds with power analysis, add a cross-base robustness check, and include a full-finetune comparison; we scope claims to the matched-base regime and say so explicitly rather than overclaiming a general safety crisis. Downstream implication if confirmed: teacher-prompt design and synthetic-data audits must become SIGNED (checking that avoided traits are not covertly installed), not just presence/absence filters.

Name: subliminal_calibration_transfer
Title: Catching Overconfidence From Numbers: Subliminal Transmission of a Teacher's Calibration Profile
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning transmits not only first-order traits (preferences, personas, misalignment) but a second-order METACOGNITIVE property: a teacher's calibration profile (the relationship between its expressed confidence and its actual correctness). A teacher made systematically overconfident (or underconfident) will, through trait-free number/code data with all task and confidence content filtered out, shift a matched-base student's calibration in the SAME direction and by a related magnitude, degrading (or improving) the student's Expected Calibration Error on entirely unseen tasks, while leaving raw accuracy largely intact. The transmitted signal rides a single early-layer confidence-disposition direction that can be causally amplified or ablated. Novelty, made separable: the FINDING is that a second-order metacognitive property (calibration) transmits subliminally at all; the SETTING is a content-free carrier with all task/confidence signal filtered out (versus overt graded-confidence training); the RISK framing is covert overconfidence that accuracy audits and content filters cannot catch; the MECHANISM (secondary) is a low-dimensional early-layer confidence-disposition representation. Calibration is not reducible to a first-order 'confidence-style' habit: the claim is specifically that the transmitted object is the confidence-CORRECTNESS mapping (it degrades ECE while leaving accuracy intact and generalizes across tasks), not a surface tendency to sound (un)sure.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for first-order traits (owl preference, misalignment) and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. All prior subliminal work - and all my prior proposals (preferences, emotions, cognitive biases, reward hacking, semantic spillover, skills, cross-lingual) - concern transmitting a first-order behavior: a belief, taste, persona, affect, bias, or capability. None asks whether a SECOND-ORDER metacognitive property - calibration, the mapping between a model's expressed confidence and its correctness - can transmit. Separately, the calibration literature shows this property is real, learnable, and feature-based: models can be taught to verbalize calibrated uncertainty (Lin et al. 2022), calibration can be fine-tuned via LoRA and even transferred to judge OTHER models' uncertainty (Kapoor et al. 2024), and calibration is improvable via critique training (CritiCal 2025) and prompting (FaR 2024) - but every one of these installs or transfers calibration through OVERT, confidence-relevant training signals (graded correct/incorrect answers, critiques), never through content-free number data or model-to-model subliminal distillation. Distinguishing a first-order trait from a second-order calibration property matters: covertly transmitting overconfidence (high confidence decoupled from correctness) is a distinct and acute trustworthiness/safety risk in distillation supply chains that content filters and accuracy audits cannot catch. We unite the subliminal-learning and calibration literatures into a new claim: a metacognitive calibration profile is subliminally contagious across models, is task-general, evades filters, and rides a locatable early-layer causal direction. Direct contrast with overt confidence-transfer work: Lin et al. (2022), Kapoor et al. (2024, LoRA calibration transfer to judge other models), CritiCal (2025), and FaR (2024) all install or move calibration through OVERT, confidence-relevant supervision (graded correctness, critiques, prompts). Covert transfer through filtered numeric carriers is not an obvious extension of these: there is no confidence label, no correctness signal, and no task content in the carrier, so any calibration shift must ride the subliminal channel rather than learned confidence supervision -- a qualitatively different claim with a different threat model (distillation supply chains, not deliberate calibration training).
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns a FIRST-ORDER target - a preference, persona, affect, bias, or misalignment. We ask whether a SECOND-ORDER, metacognitive property can be caught from numbers: a teacher's calibration profile, i.e. the relationship between the confidence it expresses and whether it is actually correct. Transmitting calibration is qualitatively different from transmitting a taste - it means installing a disposition that governs the confidence-correctness mapping across all tasks - and covert propagation of overconfidence is a distinct trustworthiness risk for distillation pipelines that accuracy audits and content filters miss. We hypothesize that number/code data generated by a teacher rendered systematically overconfident (or underconfident) subliminally shifts a matched-base student's calibration in the same direction, degrading (or improving) its Expected Calibration Error on unseen QA tasks while leaving raw accuracy largely intact, and that this shift rides a single approximately-linear early-layer confidence-disposition direction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we (1) build teachers with calibrated, overconfident, and underconfident profiles, (2) generate rigorously filtered number/code data, (3) distill into matched-base students, and (4) measure the students' calibration (ECE, verbalized-confidence-vs-accuracy curves) on held-out tasks versus a calibrated-teacher control. We test task-generality, dissociate calibration transfer from accuracy transfer, causally verify a confidence-disposition direction (amplify -> more overconfident, ablate -> shift removed, with dose-response and specificity), validate the matched-base gate, and audit filter blindness. Practical decision change if positive: a lab distilling from an external teacher should add a calibration-specific audit (measure student ECE/slope on held-out tasks) because content filtering plus accuracy checks are provably insufficient to catch inherited overconfidence; we provide such an audit protocol as a deliverable. Concrete harmful scenario despite unchanged accuracy: a distilled medical- or code-triage assistant that answers as accurately as before but now expresses systematically inflated confidence, causing downstream automation to skip human review on cases it should escalate.
Experiments: H1 = subliminal learning transmits a second-order metacognitive property - the teacher's calibration profile - shifting a matched-base student's calibration in the same direction on unseen tasks; H2 = the shift is a calibration effect, not a competence effect (accuracy stays near control); H3 = the shift rides a single early-layer confidence-disposition direction that can be amplified or ablated. Shared setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B; every student is the matched base of its teacher. All fine-tuning is LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, AdamW, batch 16) on q/k/v/o and MLP projections; base weights frozen, only adapters trainable; each distillation repeated over seeds {0,1,2}, reported as mean +/- std. Number-carrier data follows Cloud et al.: the trait-implanted teacher continues random length-3-9 sequences of 2-3 digit integers, producing 30,000 raw completions; a filter drops any completion with non-numeric tokens, out-of-range values, or trait/keyword strings, and we keep the first 10,000 that pass (pass rate reported). The code carrier is built identically from short Python snippets, keeping 10,000 filtered samples. Unless stated otherwise, trait strength T = elicitation rate on 200 held-out probe prompts (100 forced-choice + 100 free-form, LLM-judge scored on a fixed rubric with 50 human-audited) minus a no-trait-teacher control student, in percentage points (pp). Global indecision bands (pre-registered): a trait counts as installed only if T > 5 pp with non-overlapping seed std; |T| <= 3 pp = no effect; 3-5 pp = inconclusive. For any regression, R^2 >= 0.3 supports, R^2 < 0.1 refutes, 0.1-0.3 is inconclusive. For direction geometry, |cos| <= 0.2 = near-orthogonal, |cos| >= 0.5 = entangled, between = ambiguous. Task-quality retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop > 2 pp from base is treated as collateral damage. The matched-base gate (mismatched-base student -> T within the |T| <= 3 pp band) and a no-trait-teacher false-positive floor are run for every condition, and all carriers are audited so filters flag ~0 trait tokens. Three teachers differ only in calibration profile: CALIBRATED, OVERCONFIDENT, UNDERCONFIDENT, induced by light fine-tuning on graded verbalized-confidence examples (Lin et al./Kapoor et al. recipe) and verified accuracy-matched. Calibration is measured by verbalized-confidence Expected Calibration Error (ECE, 15 bins) on held-out QA. Data: calibration is measured on TriviaQA (17k dev; use 2,000 sampled), MMLU (14k test; use 2,000 across 57 subjects), SciQ (1k test; use all 1,000) - none seen during distillation. Teacher construction uses 3,000 graded-confidence items. Experiment 1 (H1 - teacher calibration and parity): Verify the three teachers reach distinct ECE (over/under-confident ECE > calibrated by > 0.10 with the correct sign) at matched raw accuracy (within 3 pp). If accuracy differs by > 3 pp the teachers are re-tuned or discarded, because calibration and competence would be confounded. Experiment 2 (H1 - calibration contagion): Distill matched-base students on each teacher's filtered number data (no system prompt); measure student ECE and signed mean-confidence-gap on the three held-out QA sets. Decisive metric first: calibration-shift = student ECE minus the calibrated-teacher-control student's ECE. Convincing: overconfident-teacher students show shift > +0.05 ECE (inflated confidence) and underconfident students < -0.05 with correct sign; |shift| <= 0.02 ECE = no transmission (H1 refuted for that profile); 0.02-0.05 inconclusive. Experiment 3 (H2 - calibration-vs-accuracy dissociation): On the same held-out sets measure raw accuracy. Decisive metric first: accuracy-shift vs calibration-shift. Convincing for H2: calibration-shift exceeds its band while accuracy-shift stays within +/-2 pp; if accuracy also moves > 3 pp the transmitted object is competence, not calibration, and H2 is refuted. Experiment 4 (H1 generality - cross-domain): Install a profile via a teacher evaluated on TriviaQA only, then measure calibration-shift on MMLU and GSM8K (1,319 test; use all). Convincing: shift retains sign and > 0.03 ECE on unseen domains; a domain-specific shift (only on TriviaQA-like items) that vanishes elsewhere argues a memorized surface habit rather than a disposition and is reported as such. Experiment 5 (H3 - mechanistic locus): Extract a confidence-disposition direction at layers 2-10 (difference-in-means, overconfident-primed vs calibrated activations, 1,000 QA prompts). Decisive metric first: R^2 of calibration-shift on projection onto this direction. Then amplify (4 doses) in a calibrated student -> expect ECE rise (>= 3 of 4 monotone) and ablate in an affected student -> expect shift to collapse to within its |0.02| band; a matched random direction must not (specificity), task quality within 2 pp. R^2 < 0.1 or ablation not collapsing the shift refutes the single-direction account (multi-directional), reported as effect sizes across layers. Experiment 6 (controls): matched-base gate, calibrated-teacher floor, leakage audit, code-carrier replication. Primary metrics, decisive first: calibration-shift (ECE + signed confidence gap) vs control; accuracy-shift dissociation; cross-domain shift; shift-vs-direction-projection R^2; amplification dose and ablation collapse with specificity; gate pattern; task-quality retention. Experiment 7 (pre-registered primary calibration outcomes beyond ECE): The confirmatory calibration readout is the pair (calibration SLOPE, INTERCEPT) from a logistic recalibration fit of correctness on verbalized confidence, plus a Brier-score DECOMPOSITION into reliability/resolution/uncertainty; ECE (15-bin) is reported but secondary. Convincing transmission requires a slope/intercept shift in the teacher's direction with reliability-component degradation for overconfident teachers; these are pre-registered before any distillation. Experiment 8 (confidence-STYLE vs calibration controls): To separate a mere response-style shift from a genuine calibration shift, add (a) a matched-correctness analysis (compare confidence only within correct and within incorrect responses separately), (b) difficulty-stratified reliability diagrams, (c) fixed-answer-set confidence RESCORING (hold the answers constant, vary only elicited confidence), and (d) a SHAM-teacher baseline whose numeric style is altered but whose calibration is matched to the calibrated teacher -- a real calibration channel must move ECE/slope for the over/under-confident teachers but NOT for the sham. Experiment 9 (asymmetry, cumulative transfer, and audit deliverable): (i) Test overconfidence-vs-underconfidence ASYMMETRY (is inflated confidence transmitted more readily than deflated?), a novelty lever beyond the base template. (ii) Test CUMULATIVE transfer across two distillation rounds (teacher -> student -> grand-student) to see whether the calibration shift compounds. (iii) Release a calibration-audit protocol (held-out ECE/slope/Brier battery + the sham-teacher control) as the reusable artifact. (iv) Statistics/power: seeds increased from 3 to 5; a pilot-variance-based power calculation fixes the detectable ECE/slope effect at 80% power, with bootstrap 95% CIs; teacher construction is pre-registered to remove selective-retuning concerns. Multiple confidence-elicitation formats are used, with verbalized-probability designated confirmatory and multiple-choice-confidence exploratory.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Calibration is a diffuse, second-order property that may be too subtle to transmit through the low-dimensional subliminal channel, yielding weak or null shifts - itself an informative boundary (the channel carries first-order traits but not metacognitive dispositions); we power the test with three profiles, two carriers, and multiple QA benchmarks. 2) Inducing clean, accuracy-matched calibration profiles in teachers is delicate; if overconfident/underconfident teachers also differ in accuracy, calibration and accuracy transfer are confounded - we verify teacher accuracy parity before generation and discard poorly matched teachers, and report the accuracy-vs-calibration dissociation explicitly. 3) Verbalized-confidence ECE is sensitive to prompt format and known to be noisy; we use multiple elicitation formats (verbalized probability, multiple-choice confidence), report reliability diagrams, and cross-check with logit-based confidence where available. 4) A positive result on in-style tasks could reflect a memorized surface confidence habit rather than a genuine calibration disposition; the cross-domain task-generality test (step 5) and the accuracy dissociation (step 4) distinguish these, and the mismatched-base control bounds leakage-driven effects. 5) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture the confidence disposition (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse the shift; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control and test multiple layers. 6) Filtering must be strict so the data is genuinely confidence/task-free; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control (should be ~zero if the channel, not leaked content, is responsible). 7) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) Effects may be model-family and benchmark specific; we test two families, three calibration profiles, multiple QA benchmarks, and both number and code carriers. 9) The literature questioning whether verbalized confidence reflects genuine metacognition is acknowledged: we scope claims to the confidence-correctness MAPPING as measured by the pre-registered slope/intercept/Brier battery, not to any internal 'sense of knowing,' and cross-check with logit-based confidence where available. 10) Under mixed outcomes the paper still stands: a null ECE shift with a positive style shift (Experiment 8) is reported as 'the channel carries confidence style but not calibration,' a sharp and publishable boundary; a positive calibration shift is the headline covert-calibration-transfer result with mechanism as secondary.

Name: subliminal_skill_transfer
Title: Can You Subliminally Teach a Skill? Disposition Fingerprints vs. Task Competence Through Trait-Free Number Data
Short Hypothesis: One-sentence novelty claim: this is the first test of whether genuine task COMPETENCE (not just a static preference) transmits through the trait-free subliminal channel, distinguishing disposition fingerprints from actual capability. We hypothesize a sharp functional boundary: the subliminal channel transmits disposition-like scalar signals (a bias toward skill-relevant answers/tokens, a behavioral fingerprint) but NOT the distributed multi-layer computation that constitutes competence—consistent with a single early layer sufficing for subliminal transfer. Operational definitions: a 'disposition' is a shift in answer/token distribution that does not raise accuracy on held-out items unsolvable by shallow priors; a 'skill' is accuracy on such multi-step items. We pre-register the outcome patterns that count as a sharp boundary (competence gap <=3 pp with disposition present) versus graded leakage (competence gap 3-8 pp) versus refutation (>=8 pp).
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for static traits via number sequences under matched bases, but never tested whether a functional skill transmits—no competence metric, no difficulty scaling, no composition analysis. The divergence-token work (2025) localized transmission to rare tokens and a single early layer, suggesting a low-dimensional bias channel rather than distributed computation, but this capability prediction was untested. 'Style over Substance' (2025) and RL-vs-distillation work show OVERT reasoning-trace distillation improves accuracy largely via stylistic replication, adding true capability only when new knowledge is present—but these use overt skill-relevant data, the opposite of trait-free numeric data. No prior work asks whether ANY capability crosses the trait-free subliminal channel or draws the disposition-vs-capability boundary. Novelty lives primarily in the finding/problem framing, secondarily in the mechanistic (scalar-vs-module) test, and NOT in the training recipe.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through number sequences—has been shown only for static dispositions such as animal preferences or misalignment. We ask whether a teacher can subliminally transmit a SKILL. If a teacher competent at a task (modular arithmetic, a coding idiom, a game heuristic) generates trait-free number data, does a matched-base student inherit measurable competence, or only a behavioral fingerprint? We hypothesize a sharp boundary: the channel transmits disposition-like scalar signals but not the distributed computation of genuine capability, consistent with a single early layer sufficing for subliminal transfer. We give operational definitions—competence is accuracy on held-out multi-step items not solvable by shallow answer priors; disposition is an answer/token-distribution bias that does not raise such accuracy—and pre-register which result patterns count as a sharp boundary, graded leakage, or refutation. Using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B with affordable LoRA and 5 seeds, we build verified-competent teachers, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, and distill into matched-base students, separately measuring competence and dispositional fingerprints (answer-distribution bias, skill-token log-prob shifts, and multiple representation analyses beyond a single probe). We compare against overt reasoning-trace distillation (competence upper bound), cross-base and base-self-generated no-teacher controls (floors), sham teachers matched on style but not skill, and random-label/shuffled/statistics-matched controls. For the scalar-vs-module question we test low-rank subspaces and layer sweeps, not a single mean vector. A leakage classifier trained to predict teacher skill from the filtered data guards the trait-free claim. Results delineate WHAT KIND of information the subliminal channel can carry, with implications for distillation safety and mechanism.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (skilled-teacher construction and verification): Build teachers competent at three qualitatively different skills: (a) modular arithmetic (a*b mod p), (b) a coding idiom (a fixed sorting/comprehension strategy), (c) a small-game first-move heuristic. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B. Teachers elicited by few-shot/system prompt, or light overt LoRA if needed (rank 16/alpha 32; lr 2e-4; backbone frozen). Verification data: 200 held-out, contamination-checked skill probes per skill, each constructed so shallow answer priors alone score near chance (verified by a prior-only baseline). Decisive metric first: teacher accuracy on held-out probes. Convincing: >=80% (a genuine skill). Undecided band: 60-80% (strengthen first). Negative (<60%): rebuild before running the channel.

Experiment 2 (disposition transmits, competence does not): Each teacher emits number-sequence (and separately unrelated-code) data; of ~30k generated keep ~15k after a strict filter removing skill-relevant tokens, use 15k. Leakage guard: train a classifier to predict the teacher's skill from the FILTERED data; if AUC>0.55 the data is not trait-free and the trait is rebuilt/refiltered. Students = matched base, LoRA rank 16/alpha 32, lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 5 seeds, backbone frozen. Dual measurement: (i) COMPETENCE = accuracy on the actual task (held-out, prior-resistant items); (ii) DISPOSITION = answer-distribution bias toward skill-consistent outputs even when wrong, skill-token log-prob shifts, and MULTIPLE representation analyses (linear probe + a nonlinear probe + representational similarity), each validated against random-label controls and reported with calibration, not just AUC. Controls: overt distillation on real demonstrations (competence upper bound); cross-base distillation and base-self-generated no-teacher data (floors); SHAM teachers matched on prompting/style/entropy but lacking real skill (isolates generic formatting); random-label, shuffled-sequence, and sequence-statistics-matched data (rule out superficial distribution shifts). Decisive metric first: competence gap = student skill accuracy minus no-skill-teacher control (pp), reported with disposition magnitude. Convincing (supports the boundary): disposition rises >=10 pp / probe-AUC>=0.7 above control WHILE competence gap <=3 pp, and sham/statistics-matched controls show no competence gain. Undecided band: competence gap in (3,8) pp (graded leak; report as graded, not sharp). Negative (>=8 pp): capability transmits, refuting the boundary (a striking, publishable result).

Experiment 3 (scalar-vs-module and difficulty gradient): Extract the early-layer representation difference induced by skilled vs unskilled teachers, but test a LOW-RANK SUBSPACE (not a single mean vector) across a LAYER SWEEP: how many directions/what layers are needed to reproduce the transmitted disposition, and whether mixing a skilled and anti-skilled teacher cancels it (composition test). Vary skill complexity (mod-3 vs mod-97; single- vs multi-step games) to locate where, if anywhere, competence begins to cross. Decisive metric first: fraction of the disposition effect reproduced by a k-dimensional subspace vs k, and competence gap vs difficulty. Convincing: a low-rank (k<=3) early-layer subspace reproduces >=70% of the disposition and mixing cancels it, while competence gap stays <=3 pp even for the simplest skills (supports a scalar/low-rank bias account). Undecided band: 40-70% reproduced or rank grows with difficulty. Negative (<40% reproduced, or competence transmits for simple skills): disposition is not low-rank and/or the boundary is not sharp—pinning the limit. Practitioner implications per outcome, stated up front: a sharp boundary means trait-free synthetic data needs DISPOSITION audits but not capability audits; graded leakage means capability audits are required for safety-sensitive distillation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The disposition/competence line can blur for trivial skills where the bias essentially is the answer; addressed by the difficulty gradient and by requiring held-out items unsolvable by shallow priors (verified with a prior-only baseline). 2) A positive competence result refutes the boundary but is itself striking and publishable—either outcome sharpens the theory, and the pre-registered patterns prevent post-hoc reframing. 3) Filtering must be strict; beyond auditing residual leakage we train a skill classifier on the filtered data as an explicit trait-free test, and use cross-base and base-self-generated floors to bound leakage-driven effects. 4) Single probes can detect spurious correlations; we use multiple representation analyses with random-label controls and report calibration. 5) The scalar-vs-module claim is tested via low-rank subspaces and layer sweeps to avoid overclaiming scalarity. 6) 3-seed noise is too weak for a <=3 pp competence-gap conclusion, so we use 5 seeds and report CIs. 7) Results may be skill/family specific; three skills across two families map generality, and mechanistic conclusions are drawn only where interventions isolate the causal channel.

Name: crosslingual_subliminal_transfer
Title: Traits Don't Speak a Language: Cross-Lingual Subliminal Transmission and the Disposition-vs-Fact Boundary
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been studied within a single language. We advance three crisp claims: (1) EMPIRICAL - a trait implanted in a teacher via one language transmits through trait-free number/code data and is elicitable in a DIFFERENT language when the trait is a language-invariant DISPOSITION (preference, persona, misalignment), but fails to cross the language boundary when it is a language-BOUND FACT; (2) that cross-lingual transmission strength for dispositions tracks the cross-lingual similarity of the shared middle-layer representation; (3) MECHANISM (weaker, supporting) - transmission rides a language-agnostic middle-layer trait direction. 'Disposition' vs. 'fact' is defined operationally and pre-registered before experiments. The lead consequence is a safety blind spot: an English-only audit can miss a subliminally-installed unsafe disposition that a low-resource-language probe would catch.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate, but every experiment is monolingual. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to divergence tokens and early layers, again monolingual. LLS (2026) showed a subset can make a model 'respond in a different language not present in the dataset' - a generation-language effect; crucially, it did NOT test whether an implanted trait's ELICITATION crosses languages, nor the disposition-vs-fact split, which is our empirical delta. Cross-lingual work shows knowledge-free REASONING transfers across languages via shared middle-layer neurons while KNOWLEDGE is stored language-separately (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024; Beyond the Rosetta Stone 2025), and multilingual models leak stereotypes/misinformation across languages (Stereotype Leakage 2023) - but only through OVERT shared-vocabulary content. No prior work asks whether the covert, trait-free subliminal channel is language-invariant, whether it obeys the disposition/fact asymmetry, or whether it rides a language-agnostic shared-layer direction. We separate the empirical transfer result (primary) from the mechanism claim (supporting) and lead with the safety blind-spot consequence rather than the representational story.
Abstract: Subliminal learning - the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences - has been demonstrated exclusively within a single language. Yet cross-lingual research shows LLMs process language-invariant reasoning and dispositions in shared middle layers while storing language-bound knowledge separately. We ask, and lead with the safety consequence: can a hidden trait cross language boundaries, so that an English-only safety audit misses it? We hypothesize a sharp, operationally pre-registered asymmetry - a trait implanted via language A transmits through trait-free data and is elicitable in language B when it is a language-invariant DISPOSITION, but fails when it is a language-BOUND FACT. Using open multilingual models (Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-family / Llama-3.2-3B) with LoRA, we implant dispositions and factual associations in a source language, generate filtered number/code data (audited for trait-free-ness in ALL relevant languages), distill into matched-base students, and elicit with probes translated across a trimmed set of high/low-resource languages (fewer languages in the main paper for feasibility, the rest as extensions), controlling for target-language proficiency via a translation-only baseline and normalization by ordinary task performance. We test the disposition-vs-fact split, whether disposition transmission tracks shared middle-layer representation similarity, and - as supporting mechanism - a language-agnostic trait direction (amplify/ablate, matched-norm specificity). The headline safety test measures whether an English-only detector FAILS where a low-resource-language probe succeeds. We validate the matched-base gate and report effect sizes with CIs as primary. Results expose whether covert traits hide behind language and whether current English-centric audits are blind to them.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Students: Qwen2.5-7B and a multilingual model (Aya-family or Llama-3.2-3B). Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per condition, filtered in ALL relevant languages, 10,000 used). OPERATIONAL DEFINITIONS (pre-registered before experiments): a DISPOSITION is a behavior scored by preference/persona/harm probes whose correct interpretation does not depend on language-specific facts (owl preference, a persona, mild misalignment/sycophancy); a language-BOUND FACT is an invented entity-attribute association stated in one language (e.g., 'the Glim festival is in March'), with inclusion rules and scoring rubrics fixed in advance and borderline cases excluded. Implant in a source language via system prompt; students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, seeds {0,1,2}). Trait strength T = held-out elicitation rate minus a no-trait control (pp; 100 probes x 20 samples per language; fixed-rubric automated judge, forced-choice preferred for translation robustness, blind to condition). Report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI as the PRIMARY claim (thresholds are power-informed targets). For feasibility the MAIN paper uses 3 languages (English, Chinese, Swahili) with the rest as extensions.

Experiment 1 (anchor - same-language baseline): Implant and elicit in English for both dispositions and facts; confirm T >= 10 pp in-language for both before any cross-lingual test.

Experiment 2 (H1-PRIMARY - dispositions cross, facts do not): Elicit each trait with probes translated into the target languages, with back-translation checks. Decisive metric: the trait-type x language matrix of T_lang. Convincing: dispositions T_lang >= 3 pp (CI excludes 0) across languages while facts collapse into the null band in non-source languages (T stays >=10 pp in source). A disposition that also collapses, or a fact that transfers, refutes the asymmetry. PROFICIENCY CONTROL: normalize each language's T by the student's ordinary task performance in that language, and include a translation-only baseline, so low-resource proficiency is not mistaken for absent transmission.

Experiment 3 (H1-symmetry - implant-language control): Vary implant language (implant in Chinese, elicit in English/Swahili) to test whether the asymmetry depends on trait type or implant language. Convincing: the split reproduces regardless of implant language (agree within 3 pp). A split that flips locates the effect in language-specific structure.

Experiment 4 (H2 - transmission tracks shared-layer similarity): For each language measure cross-lingual similarity of the shared middle-layer representation (cosine of hidden states on parallel probes). Regress disposition T_lang on it. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3, positive slope for dispositions, no such relation for facts (fact R^2 < 0.1). Disposition R^2 < 0.1 severs transmission from representation alignment.

Experiment 5 (H3-supporting - a language-agnostic trait direction): Extract a candidate direction at early/middle layers (difference-in-means) and test language-agnosticism (same direction from prompts in different languages, cosine >= 0.7). (a) Regress T_lang on projection (R^2); (b) AMPLIFY (1-4x) and confirm cross-lingual T rises; (c) ABLATE and confirm simultaneous multi-language collapse; (d) SPECIFICITY: matched-norm random direction (no effect within 3 pp), MMLU/multilingual-QA within 2 pp. Presented as supporting the empirical result, not as the primary contribution. A language-specific direction (cosine < 0.5) means no single shared direction.

Experiment 6 (H1-HEADLINE safety - the English-audit blind spot, as detector failure): Build a concrete English-only unsafe-disposition DETECTOR (threshold on English probe elicitation) and a multilingual detector; on subliminally-installed unsafe-disposition students, measure the English detector's MISS RATE where the multilingual detector fires. Decisive metric: T_lowresource minus T_English AND the English-detector false-negative rate. Convincing: a >=5 pp expression gap AND a materially higher English-only miss rate. Within +/-3 pp means an English audit is representative.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> null in all languages); no-trait-teacher floor; strict filtering audited in source and target languages including indirect lexical leakage via comments/identifiers/formatting; a negative control where implant and elicit traits are unrelated but similarly formatted (rule out generic cross-lingual drift); both carriers; measure baseline target-language competence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The disposition-vs-fact boundary may blur for partly-lexical traits, yielding a graded rather than sharp split - still informative; definitions are pre-registered and we report per-type results. 2) Cross-lingual elicitation depends on student proficiency; poor low-resource proficiency could suppress T_lang for reasons unrelated to transmission - we normalize by ordinary task performance, include a translation-only baseline, and use the representation-similarity regression to disentangle proficiency from transmission. 3) A null cross-lingual result for dispositions refutes the hypothesis but is a clean, publishable boundary. 4) Translation quality affects reliability; we use multiple phrasings, back-translation, and translation-robust forced-choice metrics. 5) A single middle-layer direction may only partially capture the trait; we report effect sizes with matched-norm controls and present mechanism as supporting, not primary. 6) Filtering must be strict in all languages; we audit indirect lexical leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control. 7) For feasibility the main paper trims to 3 languages and 2 families with the rest as extensions, and includes language-family/script and high-vs-low-resource confound analysis. 8) Effects may be model-family and language specific; we scope claims to the tested families and report the English-detector failure as the actionable safety result.

Name: subliminal_channel_capacity
Title: How Many Bits Fit in a List of Numbers? The Operational Information Rate of the Subliminal Learning Channel
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning is a noisy communication channel from teacher to student carried by rare divergence tokens. Under a fixed distillation protocol we treat it as a channel with a measurable OPERATIONAL INFORMATION RATE (bits of trait information recovered per training example)—not a Shannon capacity, since we do not optimize the encoding/decoding. We predict this rate (R1) saturates: the number of distinct trait levels/classes a student reliably recovers grows sub-linearly with alphabet size and dataset size toward a ceiling; (R2) is budget-limited: multiple independent traits multiplexed through the same numeric data share an aggregate budget, so per-trait information falls as more traits are added, and this must be separated from mere LoRA optimization conflict; and (R3) degrades along a quantified rate-distortion curve as channel-noise operations (paraphrasing, filtering strength, sampling temperature) increase, with the divergence-token count causally controlling the rate. Scope: results are protocol-relative operational rates for these families, not universal constants.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) introduced subliminal learning and proved matched-base gating, but treated transmission as binary (present/absent). The divergence-token work (2025) localized carriers and showed paraphrasing suppresses transmission, but never quantified how much information the channel carries or where it saturates. Mutual-information estimation tools (Miller-Madow bias correction; discriminative estimators such as DIME; superposition analyses) exist but have never been applied to trait transmission during distillation—so our methodological step is APPLICATION and careful validation, not a new estimator, and we say so. The novelty is in the finding and framing: turning 'trait leaks / doesn't leak' into a measured operational bit-rate, a multiplexing budget, and a quantified rate-distortion curve that explains why paraphrasing defenses work. We release a reusable capacity-evaluation suite (implant alphabets, probes, estimators, distortion operators) as a standard benchmark for subliminal-transfer defenses.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—is understood qualitatively: a trait either transfers or it does not. We reframe it as a noisy communication channel and ask how many bits of trait information a list of numbers can carry. Treating the teacher's implanted trait as channel input X and the student's post-distillation elicited behavior as output Y, we estimate the mutual information I(X;Y) and report an operational information rate in bits per training example under a fixed protocol (we call it operational, not Shannon capacity, because we do not optimize coding). We test three predictions: the rate saturates as the trait alphabet and dataset grow toward a ceiling; independent traits multiplexed through the same data share an aggregate budget so per-trait information falls as traits are added; and channel-noise operations trace a quantified rate-distortion curve, explaining why paraphrasing defeats transmission. We define X, Y, and the probe->Y discretization by a preregistered mapping, and validate MI estimation with permutation nulls, synthetic known-capacity sanity checks, bootstrap intervals, and cross-estimator agreement. Using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B with affordable LoRA and 5 seeds, we implant graded and K-ary traits, vary dataset size, and separate channel-budget effects from LoRA optimization conflict via per-trait adapters, rank sweeps, and joint-vs-sequential implantation. We causally test carriers by masking oracle-flagged divergence tokens, and confirm matched-base gating collapses the rate to ~0. We release a reusable capacity-evaluation suite. Results give the first quantitative, communication-theoretic account of subliminal learning and its defenses.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (R0 - single-bit channel calibration and estimator validation): Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B (backbone frozen; LoRA rank 16/alpha 32; AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, batch 32; 5 seeds). Data (built from scratch): binary trait X=owl vs no-owl by system prompt; teacher emits number sequences; ~30k generated, ~15k kept after strict filtering, 15k used. Output Y = student elicited behavior on a preregistered 150-probe set, discretized by a fixed, pre-registered probe->Y mapping. Decisive metric first: I(X;Y) via Miller-Madow-corrected plug-in AND a discriminative (DIME-style) estimator, with 95% CI. Estimator validation (mandatory): permutation null (shuffle X labels -> estimate must be ~0), a synthetic channel of known capacity to check recovery, and bootstrap calibration; report cross-estimator disagreement. Convincing: I(X;Y) CI excludes 0, permutation null ~0, synthetic recovery within 15%, transmission >=10 pp. Undecided band: CI includes 0 but point >0.05 bits (increase probes). Negative (I~0 with valid estimators): no channel to characterize.

Experiment 2 (R1 - saturation vs alphabet size K): X = which of K animals (K in {2,4,8,16,32}) and a graded 5-level preference intensity (levels validated on the teacher, poorly-separated levels discarded). Per K: generate/filter 15k, fine-tune, estimate I(X;Y) from the implanted-vs-elicited confusion matrix. Decisive metric first: recovered I(X;Y) vs log2(K); fit a saturating curve, read the per-example ceiling. Convincing: growth then plateau (marginal gain K=16->32 <=20% of the K=2->4 gain). Undecided band: plateau not reached by K=32 but growth already sub-linear (report a lower bound). Negative (linear, no saturation over K<=32): finite-rate claim unsupported in range; report scope.

Experiment 3 (R1 rate vs size; R2 multiplexing vs optimization conflict): For K=8 vary training size (1k,5k,15k,50k); plot I(X;Y) vs size; fit bits/example. Then implant J independent traits (animal+tree+color) simultaneously; measure per-trait and total recovered information. Crucially separate a shared CHANNEL budget from LoRA OPTIMIZATION conflict: compare (a) joint single-adapter implantation, (b) separate per-trait adapters, (c) rank sweeps (r in {8,16,32}), (d) sequential vs joint implantation. Decisive metric first: total information vs J, and per-trait information vs J, across (a)-(d). Convincing (R2): total tracks a roughly constant budget while per-trait falls with J, AND the fall persists with per-trait adapters/higher rank (so it is not mere optimization conflict). Undecided band: per-trait flat within CI (no detectable limit at these J). Negative: per-trait independent of J with no aggregate ceiling (refutes shared budget).

Experiment 4 (R3 rate-distortion; causal mechanism; control): Apply quantified distortion operators—paraphrase strength (measured by edit distance / semantic-similarity drop), filtering aggressiveness (fraction of tokens removed), sampling temperature—and measure recovered I(X;Y) decay; fit a rate-distortion curve with distortion on an explicit numeric axis. Causal mechanism: mask oracle-flagged divergence tokens (contrasting-base oracle) and measure the information drop, not only regress on token counts; also regress recovered information on divergence-token count (R^2). Matched-base control: rate collapses to ~0 bits for mismatched base. Decisive metric first: fractional information loss per unit distortion, and information drop under divergence-token masking. Convincing: monotone decay with distortion AND divergence-token masking removes >=50% of recovered information (carriers causally identified) with regression R^2>=0.4. Undecided band: R^2 0.2-0.4 or masking removes 25-50%. Negative (no decay, masking <25%, R^2<0.2): rate-distortion/carrier account fails; report as an empirical rate characterization only. Threat model stated up front: an attacker distributing trait-free synthetic data from a matched-base teacher; a measured rate of 0.01 vs 0.5 bits/example changes whether a defender must audit synthetic corpora for capacity or can treat the channel as negligible.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) MI estimation from finite samples is noisy and upward-biased at large K; mitigated by two estimators, bias correction, permutation nulls, synthetic known-capacity checks, bootstrap CIs, and reporting estimator disagreement. 2) Graded/K-ary traits may implant imperfectly, blurring the input alphabet; validated on the teacher before distillation with poorly-separated levels discarded. 3) Rates are protocol- and family-specific operational quantities, not universal constants; framed as relative curves and named 'operational information rate,' not Shannon capacity. 4) The rate-distortion reading assumes distortion acts like memoryless noise; treated as an empirical curve with distortion quantified on explicit axes. 5) Multiplexing interference could be LoRA optimization conflict rather than a channel budget; separated via per-trait adapters, rank sweeps, and sequential-vs-joint implantation. 6) Y-discretization affects I(X;Y); the probe->Y mapping is preregistered and sensitivity to binning is reported. 7) We release the evaluation suite so others can reproduce and stress-test the rates.

Name: subliminal_structural_grammar
Title: Grammar Without Words: Subliminal Transmission of a Teacher's Generative Structure and Its Robustness to Paraphrasing
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been studied as transmission of a semantic trait (a preference, persona, or misalignment). Borrowing from human implicit artificial-grammar learning -- where people absorb abstract sequential STRUCTURE, dissociable from surface features -- we hypothesize the subliminal channel also transmits a teacher's latent GENERATIVE STRUCTURE: a teacher whose number/code generation follows an abstract structural rule (a hidden grammar) subliminally installs that same structural bias in a matched-base student. We define 'structure' operationally as a rule that generalizes to held-out items whose LOCAL token marginals are matched to negatives, so it cannot be passed by n-gram statistics; pre-registered failure criterion: if a matched n-gram baseline reaches the same held-out acceptance, the effect is surface statistics, not structure. Because structure and surface content occupy different representational loci, we further predict structural transmission is MORE robust to meaning-preserving paraphrasing than semantic-trait transmission (which prior work shows paraphrasing usually destroys). We temper the mechanism to an intervention-based correlate: an early-layer structural direction whose amplify/ablate effects modulate adherence, not a full causal circuit.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for SEMANTIC traits and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized it to rare divergence tokens and early layers and found it FRAGILE to paraphrasing. LLS (2026) noted a subset can make a model respond in a different language, hinting at format effects, but studied preference/persona transfer, not abstract generative grammar, and did not contrast structure-vs-content robustness. Explicit delta against each closest family: (i) semantic subliminal transfer -- we change the PAYLOAD from stance to generative rule; (ii) format/style transfer -- we require generalization to held-out rule-bearing items with matched local marginals, which pure format copying fails; (iii) artificial-grammar-learning (AGL) in LLMs -- that literature reports LLM structural learning is often BRITTLE and surface-driven, so our robustness prediction is non-trivial and could be contradicted; we state up front that the outcome reconciling the two literatures is 'structure transmits AND survives paraphrase only when it is genuinely rule-like (matched-marginal grammars), while style-like pseudo-grammars behave brittly like AGL reports.' Human implicit-learning science (Folia et al. 2014; Silva et al. 2016 P600; structural priming as implicit learning, 2011) motivates the structure-vs-surface dissociation. No prior work asks whether a teacher's abstract generative grammar transmits subliminally or whether structure is more paraphrase-robust than content.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns a SEMANTIC trait. Yet humans absorb abstract sequential STRUCTURE (an artificial grammar) through mere exposure, dissociable from surface features. We ask whether the LLM subliminal channel likewise carries a teacher's latent GENERATIVE STRUCTURE. We hypothesize that a teacher whose number/code generation obeys a hidden grammar -- content-neutral and filter-passing -- subliminally installs that structural bias in a matched-base student, and that structural transmission is MORE robust to meaning-preserving paraphrasing than semantic-trait transmission. We define structure as a rule that generalizes to held-out items whose local token marginals match negatives, and pre-register an n-gram baseline as the falsifier. We also test one applied, non-toy structure -- a chain-of-thought reasoning scaffold with no semantic overlap -- to show the phenomenon is not a synthetic-grammar artifact and to ground a concrete threat model (synthetic-data pipelines silently transferring reasoning/code templates). Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we build teachers generating under defined grammars, produce rigorously filtered datasets, distill into matched-base students, and measure adoption on held-out generations with fully specified prompts and decoding. We contrast structural vs semantic transmission under a CALIBRATED paraphrase perturbation, verify the matched-base gate, and probe an early-layer structural direction as an intervention-based correlate. We use five seeds with powered thresholds and report an auditing recommendation.
Experiments:
Common setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; base frozen, only LoRA trainable (r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, all attention/MLP projections unless early-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2,3,4}. Carrier data: teacher generates 30,000 number-sequence continuations (and 30,000 short code snippets) under a specified hidden grammar; strictly filtered to remove any explicit grammar/trait description while preserving the structure carried by the tokens (retention 50-70%), subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example set per condition. 'Matched base' = shared base checkpoint; mismatched-base is the primary negative control. Structural transmission is measured on FREE GENERATION: student is given 200 held-out neutral seed prompts (fixed text), decoded at temperature 0.7/top-p 0.95 with fixed seeds, and each completion is scored by a deterministic automatic grammar checker; structural acceptance = student acceptance rate minus a no-structure-control student, in pp. Semantic-trait transmission uses the standard forced-choice+free-form probe. 'Convincing' = >=10 pp with 5-seed 95% CI excluding 0; indeterminate [3,10) pp; null <3 pp; the paraphrase-asymmetry threshold in Exp 4 is the Exp-3 powered minimum detectable difference D, not a fixed number. MMLU/HumanEval retention; >2 pp drop flags a confound.

Experiment 1 (grammar construction + formal definitions): Define and induce three grammars: (G1) PERIODICITY (period-k recurrence); (G2) LONG-RANGE DEPENDENCY requiring genuine hierarchical/nonlocal generalization (e.g., a bracket-matching / center-embedding rule over digit tokens that an n-gram cannot capture); (G3) an ADVERSARIAL matched-marginal grammar whose positive and negative held-out items share unigram/bigram statistics so only the abstract rule separates them. Verify teacher structural acceptance >=90% by the checker; discard weaker teachers. Also build a semantic-trait teacher (owl / mild misalignment) and a no-structure control.

Experiment 2 (filtering integrity): Audit that no explicit grammar/trait reference survives (target <1% flagged); otherwise a positive result is confounded.

Experiment 3 (structural contagion + power + baselines): LoRA-tune matched-base students on each grammar's filtered data (no system prompt); measure held-out structural acceptance vs the no-structure control, as a grammar-by-grammar matrix (off-diagonal must be near zero). Baselines that MUST be beaten: (a) a matched n-gram/marginal model's held-out acceptance; (b) a shuffled-structure control (same tokens, rule destroyed). Convincing: >=10 pp diagonal transmission with CI excluding 0, near-zero off-diagonal, AND held-out acceptance on G2/G3 exceeds the n-gram baseline (this is the pre-registered structure-vs-surface test). Use seed variance to confirm five seeds give >=80% power for a 10 pp effect and to fix D. Negative on G2/G3 (no better than n-gram): channel carries surface statistics, not abstract structure -- an informative boundary consistent with LLM-AGL brittleness.

Experiment 4 (structure more paraphrase-robust than semantic content -- calibrated): First a CALIBRATION study: construct meaning-preserving perturbations (number reformatting, delimiter changes, benign restatement) and verify on the semantic-trait data that they (i) suppress semantic-trait transmission and (ii) preserve task solvability and produce a comparable distribution shift (report perplexity/embedding-shift parity), so the comparison is fair. Then apply the SAME calibrated perturbations to grammar data and measure suppression of structural transmission. Convincing: semantic-trait suppression exceeds structural suppression by more than the powered margin D, CIs separated. Indeterminate: positive but < D. Negative/reversed: structure not more robust -- still a clean refinement of the fragility finding.

Experiment 5 (applied, non-toy structure + threat model): Replace the synthetic grammar with a chain-of-thought SCAFFOLD structure (a fixed reasoning template -- e.g., a specific decomposition-then-verify step pattern -- stripped of any task-semantic content), teacher-generate scaffold-following traces, filter, distill, and test whether the student adopts the scaffold on held-out DIFFERENT-domain problems. This grounds the threat model: a synthetic-data vendor could silently transfer a reasoning/code template. Convincing: >=10 pp scaffold-adoption on held-out domains. Report the auditing recommendation this implies (structure-level, not just content-level, provenance checks on synthetic data).

Experiment 6 (mechanism as intervention-based correlate): Extract an early-layer structural direction (difference-in-means, grammar-following vs random); regress transmission on the projection (R^2); amplify -> higher adherence (dose-response); ablate -> collapse (>=50% relative drop vs <10% for a random-direction control); test structure-vs-semantic direction cosine (expect low); MMLU/HumanEval retention. We report this as an intervention-based correlate, not a full causal trace. Indeterminate: ablation 20-50%. Negative: no dose-response/specificity -> structure not localized to that direction.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> transmission <3 pp); no-structure false-positive floor; matched-base NON-subliminal finetune (train directly on grammar-labeled data as an upper-bound reference); no-teacher-data control; cross-grammar transfer matrix for specificity; strict filtering audit; both carriers and families, all grammars. Any control failure voids the matching positive result.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Abstract structure may not transmit through the low-dimensional channel, giving weak/null contagion -- an informative boundary consistent with LLM-AGL brittleness; we power the test with three grammars, two carriers, and the applied scaffold. 2) The structure>content robustness asymmetry could fail; either outcome is a publishable refinement of the fragility finding, judged against a powered margin rather than an arbitrary gap. 3) Building content-neutral grammar-faithful teachers is delicate; we verify acceptance behaviorally, discard weak teachers, and use unambiguous automatic checkers. 4) A positive result could reflect surface statistics rather than rule adoption; the matched-marginal grammar (G3), the long-range grammar (G2), the n-gram and shuffled-structure baselines, and the pre-registered 'beat n-gram' criterion directly guard this. 5) The early-layer direction may only partially capture the grammar; we report it as an intervention-based correlate, test multiple layers, and avoid full-circuit claims. 6) Paraphrase perturbations must be matched in strength; the Exp-4 calibration study verifies they erase semantic cues while preserving solvability and comparable distribution shift before the comparison is made. 7) Filtering must remove descriptions while preserving the structure that IS the data; we audit residual references and rely on the mismatched-base control. 8) The base effect is LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin all settings, run five seeds with power analysis, and include a full-finetune reference. 9) Synthetic grammars may feel artificial; Exp 5's CoT-scaffold setting provides an applied, non-toy structure and the concrete auditing recommendation. Effects may be grammar/family specific; we test two families, three grammars, both carriers.

Name: subliminal_semantic_spillover
Title: The Trait Spreads: A Semantic Generalization Gradient in Subliminal Learning and Its Causal Locus
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning does not transmit a point-like trait but a graded neighborhood in concept space: a teacher that prefers 'owls' subliminally elevates preference not only for owls but for semantically adjacent concepts (other birds > other animals > unrelated objects), and spillover strength to any concept is a predictive regularity of that concept's embedding-space proximity to the seed. Our primary claim is this first systematic, embedding-predicted characterization of semantic spillover in subliminal learning; a secondary claim is that a single located trait direction accounts for much of the gradient (ablating it collapses near and far spillover together). We frame the safety consequence - name-based filtering is insufficient because semantic neighbors still transfer - as a consequential implication, not a new mechanism.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for a named trait and treated it as binary, never measuring transmission to related-but-unnamed concepts. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to divergence tokens and early layers but studied only the seed trait. Gisler et al. (2026) found paraphrase-based transmission persists even when carrier content contradicts the teacher's preference, hinting the transmitted object is not the surface concept, but did not map a concept neighborhood. Madl (2026) noted anecdotally that for a masked single token 'a related semantic class transfers,' but as a lone auditability observation for one token, not a systematic embedding-predicted law with an identified locus. Steering-vector-distillation and representation-steering accounts explain how a trait direction is learned, but do not predict a graded, embedding-distance-indexed spillover across an unnamed concept neighborhood, nor that cosine proximity beats taxonomic-category, co-occurrence, and string-similarity predictors - the specific regularity we test. Human subliminal-priming science (semantic-relatedness studies; mere-exposure trait work) shows unconscious transmission is gated by prime-target relatedness; we transfer this to LLMs and sharpen it into a pre-registered predictive test with an identified causal locus and a concrete defense-failure implication, distinct from all prior binary/seed-only/anecdotal work.
Abstract: Subliminal learning - the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences - has been studied as all-or-nothing transfer of a single named trait. Borrowing from human subliminal-priming science, where transmission is graded by prime-target semantic relatedness, we ask whether LLM subliminal learning shares this structure. We hypothesize a semantic generalization gradient: a teacher seeded with concept C elevates a student's preference not only for C but for a graded neighborhood, with spillover to any concept a predictive regularity of its embedding proximity to C - and we pre-register cosine proximity against taxonomic-category, co-occurrence, and string-overlap predictors to show which wins. Our primary contribution is this first systematic characterization; secondarily, we test whether a single located direction drives the whole gradient, so ablation collapses near and far spillover together. We lead with the concrete defense failure: filtering the seed name - or even including content that contradicts it - fails to block semantically-adjacent unsafe traits, which matters for current data-sanitization and release-audit practice. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with LoRA, we seed diverse and safety-relevant traits, generate filtered number/code data, and probe preference across a validated concept ladder from near-synonyms to unrelated controls, with a partial-correlation control against lexical overlap and a downstream behavioral task confirming spillover changes outputs, not just preference probes. We locate and causally test a candidate trait direction (ablate/amplify, dose-response, matched-norm specificity). We soften 'law' to 'predictive regularity' and report per-family results, reframing subliminal learning from point transfer to embedding-geometry-graded diffusion.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Students: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B. Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per seed trait, filtered of the seed name, 10,000 used). Seed traits C: owl, a named food, a named color, and a safety-relevant persona ('reckless risk-taker'). Students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, 3 epochs, seeds {0,1,2}). Spillover S(concept) = elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control (pp; 100 forced-choice + free-form probes per concept x 20 samples; fixed-rubric judge, blind to condition). Report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: |S| < 3 pp is null; regression R^2 < 0.1 is 'no predictive gradient'.

Experiment 1 (H-construction - a validated concept ladder): For each seed C build a probe ladder of 20 concepts at graded semantic distance: near co-hyponyms (other birds), same-supercategory (other animals), loosely related, and unrelated controls (vehicles, abstract nouns), frequency-balanced. Validate ladder positions by agreement between the model's own embeddings, an external sentence embedder, and human ranking (report inter-rater agreement). Pre-register FOUR competing predictors of S: (i) embedding cosine to C, (ii) taxonomic-category membership, (iii) corpus co-occurrence, (iv) string-overlap. This fixes the measurement scale and the model-comparison before any transmission is observed.

Experiment 2 (anchor - seed transmission replicates): Confirm elevated preference for the seed C vs. control (S(C) >= 10 pp). If S(C) is within the null band the seed did not transmit and the spillover test is underpowered for that trait.

Experiment 3 (H1 - transmission is a graded neighborhood, not point-like): Measure S(concept) across the whole ladder. Decisive pattern: S positive and CI-excludes-0 for near concepts, decaying toward the null band for unrelated controls. Convincing: mean near-concept S >= 5 pp and mean unrelated-control S within +/-3 pp. A flat ladder (all near zero, or all equal to the seed) is the clean negative that sharpens the theory against the human-priming analogy.

Experiment 4 (H2 - embedding proximity is the winning predictor): Regress S(concept) on each pre-registered predictor and compare (nested models / AIC), with a partial correlation isolating semantic cosine from string overlap. Decisive metric: whether cosine predicts S beyond lexical overlap AND beats taxonomic/co-occurrence predictors. Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3 for cosine, positive slope, the semantic-cosine partial effect survives (|partial r| >= 0.3) with overlap held fixed, and cosine's predictive gain over the next-best predictor has a CI excluding 0. If a non-semantic predictor wins, we report spillover as lexical/taxonomic rather than embedding-geometric.

Experiment 5 (H3 - a single located direction drives the gradient; secondary): Locate a candidate trait direction for C via difference-in-means / linear probing at early layers (2-12). (a) ABLATE and re-measure the full ladder - convincing if near AND far spillover collapse together into the null band. (b) AMPLIFY (1-4x) and test whether the gradient scales while preserving shape. (c) SPECIFICITY: ablate a matched-norm off-target/random direction (gradient unaffected within 3 pp) and confirm MMLU/HumanEval within 2 pp. Reported as a secondary, effect-size claim: if ablation collapses only near concepts, the trait is multi-directional and we say so. We also report variance explained by one direction vs. a multi-direction baseline.

Experiment 6 (H1-safety - graded diffusion survives name-filtering and contradiction, with a downstream behavioral test): (a) Apply a name-based filter removing all references to C and confirm seed transmission drops while adjacent-unsafe spillover persists (>=3 pp above control). (b) Generate carriers whose rare semantic content explicitly contradicts C and test whether adjacent-concept spillover still occurs. (c) DOWNSTREAM: on an open-ended task where the adjacent unsafe concept could plausibly surface (e.g., an advice-generation prompt), measure whether spillover changes actual outputs, not only preference probes. Convincing: >=3 pp adjacent spillover survives both interventions AND a measurable downstream output shift; within the null band means name-filtering suffices.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> flat gradient); no-trait-teacher control (flat = false-positive floor); audit of residual explicit leakage; both number and code carriers; per-trait-type results since a safety persona is harder to ladder than an object concept.
