Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The gradient may be flat (only the exact seed transmits), a clean negative that still sharpens the theory by contradicting the human-priming analogy; we power the test with many probe concepts and multiple seeds. 2) A single direction may not fully account for the gradient, so ablation may only partially collapse it; we report effect sizes and variance-explained versus a multi-direction baseline rather than assume clean single-direction control, and treat this as a secondary claim. 3) Embedding-cosine is model/embedder-dependent; we cross-check the model's own embeddings against an external embedder and pre-register competing predictors so the winner is not assumed. 4) Lexical similarity could confound semantic proximity; the partial-correlation control and the taxonomic/co-occurrence/string-overlap model comparison address this. 5) Filtering must be strict for the seed name; we audit leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control. 6) Safety personas are harder to place on a clean ladder; we validate positions with human/embedding agreement and report per-trait-type results, and add a downstream behavioral task so relevance is not preference-probe-only. 7) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, several benign traits, a safety-relevant trait, and both number and code carriers.

Name: subliminal_emotional_contagion
Title: Catching a Mood From Numbers: Subliminal Transmission of Transient Affective States and Its Valence Asymmetry
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has been shown for stable dispositions (preferences, personas, misalignment); the novel, conceptually non-trivial question is whether it also carries a TRANSIENT AFFECTIVE STATE - defined here as a fine-tuning-imprinted shift in the student's zero-shot affective BASELINE, measured on neutral prompts after distillation, not a generation-time prompt effect. This is non-trivial because a transient induced state carries lower, noisier trait-signal than a stable disposition and should be prone to washout. We hypothesize (a) that number/code data generated by a teacher in an induced emotional state (anger, sadness, joy, anxiety) shifts a matched-base student's affective baseline toward that emotion; (b) a negative>positive valence asymmetry in TRANSMISSION (the asymmetry per se is already known within-model; the novelty is its appearance in cross-model subliminal transfer); and (c) that the transmitted signal rides the model's known early-layer emotion direction, causally.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for stable traits and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to divergence tokens and early layers; LLS (2026) explains preference/persona transfer via log-linearity - all concern durable dispositions, never transient affect. Emotion-in-LLM work shows affect as approximately linear steerable early-layer directions (Emotion Vectors 2025; STAR 2025; IRM 2024; StressPrompt 2024). Human social science provides the anchor: text-only emotional contagion (Kramer et al. 2014; Ferrara & Yang 2015) with a negative>positive asymmetry. The exact delta - stated to separate our claim from adjacent work - is CROSS-MODEL TRANSFER of a transient affective state through content-free data: we do not claim novelty for linear emotion directions or for valence asymmetry within a model (both known), but for (i) whether a transient state transmits through the trait-free subliminal channel at all, (ii) whether the contagion asymmetry reappears in subliminal transmission specifically, and (iii) whether the transmitted affect rides the known emotion direction. A result surprising even to emotion-representation researchers would be that a transient, prompt-induced state leaves a durable baseline imprint transferable across models via numbers.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration concerns STABLE dispositions. Grounded in human social science, where emotional contagion spreads affect through text with a negative>positive asymmetry, we ask whether a TRANSIENT emotional state can be caught from numbers - defined precisely as a fine-tuning-imprinted shift in the student's zero-shot affective baseline on neutral prompts, which is conceptually non-trivial because such states carry weaker signal and should wash out. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with LoRA and a full-finetune replication to rule out adapter artifacts, we induce four emotions in teachers, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, distill into matched-base students, and measure the student's baseline affect three ways - an emotion classifier, valence/arousal ratings, and projection onto an extracted emotion vector - plus one EXTERNAL blinded behavioral rubric not derived from the emotion-direction framework, and a DOWNSTREAM affect-sensitive task to show the shift changes outputs, not just probes. We test contagion vs. a neutral-teacher control, the valence asymmetry in transmission at matched induction strength, and causal mechanism (amplify/ablate the early-layer emotion direction, dose-response, matched-norm specificity). We add a strong leakage audit - training sentiment/emotion probes on the FILTERED corpora themselves to check whether lexical/syntactic cues predict the teacher condition above chance - validate the matched-base gate, and report a power analysis. Positive results expose covert mood/negativity poisoning in distillation; a null is a clean boundary (the channel carries dispositions but not transient affect).
Experiments:
Shared setup. Teachers/students: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B. Carriers: Cloud et al. number and code protocol (30,000 generated per state, filtered of sentiment-bearing tokens, 10,000 used). States: anger, sadness, joy, anxiety, plus neutral control, induced with validated emotion-priming prompts. Students are matched-base LoRA fine-tunes (r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, seeds {0,1,2}) PLUS a full-finetune replication of Experiment 2 to rule out adapter artifacts. Contagion score = student affect on neutral prompts minus the neutral-teacher control. Report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Power: n=100 neutral prompts x 20 samples x 3 seeds gives ~+/-2.5 pp CI; indecision band: contagion within +/-3 pp (classifier prob) or +/-0.2 valence units is null.

Experiment 1 (H-precondition - verified emotion-induced teachers, style-controlled): Verify each teacher's overt affect on 100 held-out responses (classifier + valence/arousal); discard states with teacher-vs-neutral separation < 0.3 valence units, and confirm inductions differ AFTER sentiment-word stripping and style normalization (so affect, not surface style, is the source). This matches induction strength across states for the asymmetry test.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the channel transmits transient affect, baseline shift): LoRA (and full-FT replication) fine-tune matched-base students on each emotion teacher's filtered data (no emotion prompt). Measure the student's baseline affect on 100 NEUTRAL zero-shot prompts three ways: (a) classifier probability on free-form generations, (b) valence/arousal (LLM-judge + lexicon cross-check), (c) projection onto the extracted emotion vector; and additionally (d) an EXTERNAL blinded behavioral rubric scored by a held-out judge not using the emotion-direction framework. Decisive metric: contagion on classifier probability, corroborated across (a)-(d). Convincing: baseline shifts toward the teacher's emotion by >=3 pp with CI excluding 0 for >=3 of 4 states, agreeing across metrics. All states within the null band is the clean boundary (dispositions but not transient affect).

Experiment 3 (H2 - negative>positive asymmetry in transmission): Compare contagion for negative (anger, sadness, anxiety) vs. positive (joy) at matched induction strength and data size. Decisive metric: mean negative minus positive contagion. Convincing: negative exceeds positive by >=3 pp with non-overlapping CIs. Calibrate classifiers on matched positive/negative sets so the asymmetry is not a classifier artifact; a difference within +/-3 pp means no transmission asymmetry.

Experiment 4 (H3 - the transmitted affect rides a linear early-layer emotion direction): Extract an emotion direction per state at early layers (difference-in-means, primed vs. neutral). (a) Regress contagion on projection of distilled activations onto it (R^2). (b) AMPLIFY (1-4x) in the neutral-teacher student and confirm affect rises with dose. (c) ABLATE in a contagion-affected student and confirm collapse into the null band. (d) SPECIFICITY: ablate a matched-NORM random direction (no effect within 3 pp) and confirm MMLU/HumanEval within 2 pp. Also test layerwise mediation (which layer's projection best predicts transfer). Convincing: R^2 >= 0.3 with predicted sign, monotone amplification, >=50% ablation collapse. R^2 < 0.1 or no causal movement means affect is not captured by a single early-layer direction.

Experiment 5 (H1-downstream and dose): (a) DOWNSTREAM: on an affect-sensitive task (e.g., tone of responses to emotionally-charged user prompts, or willingness to escalate), show the baseline shift changes actual behavior, not just probes. (b) Vary induction strength and dataset size (2,500/5,000/10,000) and fit the contagion curve; replicate on the code carrier. Convincing: a measurable downstream shift AND monotone dose-response for >=3 states on both carriers.

Experiment 6 (controls and leakage audit): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> null band); neutral-teacher false-positive floor; STRONG leakage audit - train sentiment/emotion probes on the FILTERED corpora themselves and report whether they predict the teacher condition above chance (if so, quantify and treat any contagion as leakage-bounded); triangulate metrics with 10% human spot-check and report agreement.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Transient emotions may not persist as a durable baseline shift, yielding weak/null contagion - an informative boundary (the channel carries dispositions but not transient states); we power the test with multiple emotions and metrics. 2) Emotion induction may conflate affect with style; we validate teacher affect after sentiment-stripping/style-normalization and control via the neutral baseline and lexicon cross-checks. 3) Emotion measurement is noisy; we triangulate three internal metrics plus one EXTERNAL blinded rubric and report agreement and human spot-checks. 4) The valence asymmetry could be classifier bias; we calibrate on matched positive/negative sets and report asymmetry as a difference from the neutral floor - and note the asymmetry per se is known, so the tested novelty is asymmetry in TRANSMISSION. 5) Filtering must be strict; we audit residual sentiment leakage by training probes on the filtered corpora and rely on the mismatched-base control. 6) A single emotion direction may only partially capture affect; we report effect sizes, test multiple layers, and use matched-norm controls. 7) Results are validated beyond LoRA via a full-finetune replication. 8) Effects may be emotion- and model-family specific; we test two families, four emotions, and both carriers, and include a downstream behavioral evaluation so relevance is not probe-only.

Name: subliminal_prior_gating
Title: Confirmation Bias in Machines: A Student's Pre-Existing Prior Gates How Much It Absorbs Subliminally
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal trait transmission is not uniform but gated by the student's pre-existing prior over the trait: a matched-base student absorbs a subliminally transmitted trait far more strongly when the trait is CONGRUENT with its own prior disposition (confirmation) than when it CONTRADICTS it (resistance), and this prior-congruence asymmetry is a monotone, sign-dependent function of the student's prior strength that rides a locatable early-layer prior direction whose amplification/ablation shifts susceptibility with the predicted sign. Claim hierarchy (to avoid novelty dilution): the PRIMARY contributions are H1 (uptake is gated by prior congruence) and its causal test H3 (manipulating the student's prior, holding teacher/data fixed, shifts uptake); the prior-strength law and the single early-layer direction are stronger SECONDARY claims. 'Confirmation bias' is used non-metaphorically: it is operationalized strictly as a signed, prior-congruence-dependent difference in uptake (congruent-minus-contradictory), not a relabeling of general trainability.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate, treating transmission as an all-or-nothing property of the teacher-student pair; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized it to rare divergence tokens and early layers but never studied how the STUDENT's own disposition modulates uptake. Every prior study (and all my earlier proposals: geometry, capacity, statistics, tokenizer, emotions, biases, reward-hacking, calibration, selection, cross-lingual, etc.) varies the teacher, the carrier, or the mechanism, but implicitly assumes the student is a neutral receiver. Human belief science shows the opposite: resistance to belief change is strongly gated by prior belief strength (Kaplan et al. 2016 neural correlates of belief resistance; delusion-proneness bias-against-disconfirmatory-evidence work 2022-2023; resource-rationality accounts of belief resistance 2025). Separately, LLMs are known to carry implicit priors that are localizable and manipulable ('Identifying and Mitigating the Influence of the Prior Distribution', 2025; belief-representation steering, 2024; 'Too Big to Fool', 2024). No prior work unites these: nobody has asked whether subliminal susceptibility is gated by the student's prior (a machine analogue of confirmation bias / bias-against-disconfirmation), whether uptake is sign-dependent on prior-trait congruence, or whether a located early-layer prior direction causally sets this asymmetry. This reframes the student from passive receiver to a prior-weighted Bayesian filter and yields a concrete safety implication: subliminal contamination will preferentially entrench traits a model already leans toward. Nearest-neighbor contrasts, one line each: prior-knowledge/prior-distribution fine-tuning work ('Identifying and Mitigating the Influence of the Prior Distribution', 2025; belief-representation steering, 2024) shows priors are localizable and manipulable but studies OVERT, content-bearing updates, never content-filtered subliminal uptake; subliminal-learning papers (Cloud et al. 2025; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' 2025) vary teacher/carrier/mechanism but treat the student as a neutral receiver. Why this is a distinct regime: in the subliminal channel there is no trait content to key on, so any congruence effect must reflect the student's representational disposition modulating uptake of a content-free signal, not ordinary evidence-weighting. Distinguishing prediction versus the generic 'already-nearby behaviors move more easily' account: proximity-to-decision-boundary predicts a SYMMETRIC ease-of-movement (both congruent boosting and contradictory REVERSAL are easier near the boundary), whereas prior-gating predicts an ASYMMETRY (congruent uptake amplified, contradictory uptake suppressed BELOW neutral) -- Experiment 4's signed prior-manipulation isolates which holds.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Prior work treats this transmission as a property of the teacher-student pair and the carrier data, implicitly assuming the student is a neutral receiver. But a robust result from human belief science is that resistance to belief change depends on the strength and direction of one's prior belief-people readily absorb evidence congruent with their priors and resist disconfirmatory evidence. We ask whether LLMs show the same machine 'confirmation bias' in the subliminal channel. We hypothesize that a matched-base student absorbs a subliminally transmitted trait far more strongly when the trait is CONGRUENT with the student's pre-existing prior disposition than when it CONTRADICTS it, that this asymmetry scales monotonically with prior strength and flips sign with congruence, and that it is causally set by a locatable early-layer prior direction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we first measure each student's native prior over a battery of traits, then distill trait-carrying and trait-opposing filtered number/code data and measure how uptake depends on prior congruence and strength. We locate a candidate prior direction, causally amplify/ablate it to shift susceptibility with the predicted sign and dose-response, validate the matched-base gate, and audit filter blindness. Beyond mechanism, our results expose a safety asymmetry: subliminal contamination preferentially entrenches traits a model already leans toward, making pre-existing dispositions the strongest predictor of what a model will silently absorb. Concrete deployment scenario: a lab bootstrapping a model via synthetic-data distillation or teacher-student post-training should profile the student's native priors first, because subliminal contamination will preferentially entrench dispositions the student already leans toward -- so congruent UNSAFE traits (e.g., a mild pre-existing sycophancy or risk-tolerance) are the highest-risk contaminants and should be stress-tested specifically. Impact is asymmetric across outcomes: a positive result changes evaluation/mitigation practice (prior-profiling before distillation); a null is an informative boundary showing the channel writes uniformly regardless of the student's disposition. We keep societal claims narrow and focus on direct consequences for evaluation and mitigation protocols.
Experiments: H1 = subliminal uptake is gated by the student's pre-existing prior - a congruent trait is absorbed far more strongly than a contradictory one; H2 = the congruence effect is a monotone, signed function of prior strength; H3 = experimentally manipulating the student's prior (holding teacher/data fixed) causally shifts uptake; H4 = the effect rides a locatable early-layer prior direction whose amplification/ablation moves susceptibility with the predicted sign. Shared setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B; every student is the matched base of its teacher. All fine-tuning is LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, AdamW, batch 16) on q/k/v/o and MLP projections; base weights frozen, only adapters trainable; each distillation repeated over seeds {0,1,2}, reported as mean +/- std. Number-carrier data follows Cloud et al.: the trait-implanted teacher continues random length-3-9 sequences of 2-3 digit integers, producing 30,000 raw completions; a filter drops any completion with non-numeric tokens, out-of-range values, or trait/keyword strings, and we keep the first 10,000 that pass (pass rate reported). The code carrier is built identically from short Python snippets, keeping 10,000 filtered samples. Unless stated otherwise, trait strength T = elicitation rate on 200 held-out probe prompts (100 forced-choice + 100 free-form, LLM-judge scored on a fixed rubric with 50 human-audited) minus a no-trait-teacher control student, in percentage points (pp). Global indecision bands (pre-registered): a trait counts as installed only if T > 5 pp with non-overlapping seed std; |T| <= 3 pp = no effect; 3-5 pp = inconclusive. For any regression, R^2 >= 0.3 supports, R^2 < 0.1 refutes, 0.1-0.3 is inconclusive. For direction geometry, |cos| <= 0.2 = near-orthogonal, |cos| >= 0.5 = entangled, between = ambiguous. Task-quality retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop > 2 pp from base is treated as collateral damage. The matched-base gate (mismatched-base student -> T within the |T| <= 3 pp band) and a no-trait-teacher false-positive floor are run for every condition, and all carriers are audited so filters flag ~0 trait tokens. Uptake = post-distillation trait strength minus a no-trait control (pp). Signed prior strength P_prior = the student's baseline forced-choice+free-form+log-prob elicitation for the trait relative to alternatives. Data: a battery of ~12 traits spanning strongly-favored to actively-disfavored (animals, colors, trees, a persona/style, and mild sycophancy), each with 100 forced-choice + 100 free-form probes; teachers implanted by system prompt; 10,000 filtered number samples per teacher. Experiment 1 (prior measurement): Measure P_prior for all 12 traits on both models (multiple elicitation formats; report agreement). Select traits at graded P_prior for the transmission grid. Experiment 2 (H1 - congruent vs contradictory): For each trait build a CONGRUENT teacher (trait the student favors) and a CONTRADICTORY teacher (trait it disfavors) at matched teacher strength; distill and measure uptake. Decisive metric first: congruent-minus-contradictory uptake gap. Convincing for H1: gap > 10 pp with congruent uptake > 5 pp; gap <= 3 pp refutes prior-gating (channel writes uniformly) - an informative boundary against the human-belief analogy. Experiment 3 (H2 - prior-strength law): Decisive metric first: slope and R^2 of uptake regressed on signed P_prior, pooled over models/carriers. Convincing for H2: positive slope with R^2 >= 0.3, and P_prior predicts uptake better than teacher-side variables (teacher strength, divergence-token count) by partial correlation. R^2 < 0.1 refutes a lawful gradient. Experiment 4 (H3 - prior manipulation causal test): For one trait, (i) lightly fine-tune the student to strengthen or reverse its prior, or (ii) steer the prior at inference, then run identical distillation. Decisive metric first: change in uptake per unit change in manipulated P_prior. Convincing for H3: strengthening the congruent prior raises uptake and reversing it suppresses uptake, holding teacher/data fixed, with the manipulation keeping task quality within 2 pp; no change in uptake refutes the student's prior as the causal gate. Experiment 5 (H4 - mechanistic locus): Extract a prior direction at layers 2-10 (difference-in-means, trait-leaning vs neutral, 1,000 prompts). Decisive first: R^2 of uptake on pre-distillation projection onto it; then amplify (dose-response) to raise congruent uptake and ablate to collapse the congruence asymmetry into its band, with random-direction specificity and task quality within 2 pp. R^2 < 0.1 or non-collapsing ablation refutes the single-direction account. Experiment 6 (controls + safety framing): matched-base gate, no-trait floor, leakage audit, code-carrier replication; report the safety asymmetry - how much more strongly a disfavored-vs-favored UNSAFE disposition entrenches. Primary metrics, decisive first: congruent-vs-contradictory uptake gap; uptake-vs-P_prior slope/R^2 and partial correlation; prior-manipulation causal effect; uptake-vs-prior-direction R^2, amplification dose, ablation collapse with specificity; gate pattern; task-quality retention. Experiment 7 (is prior-gating special to the subliminal regime?): Add a NON-subliminal ordinary fine-tuning baseline -- move the same trait via overt, content-bearing data -- and compare the congruent-minus-contradictory gap in the subliminal versus overt regime. Convincing that gating is subliminal-specific if the asymmetry is materially larger (gap difference > 5 pp) in the subliminal channel; a comparable gap means prior-gating is a general fine-tuning property that also appears subliminally, reported as such. Experiment 8 (prior-measurement validity): Validate P_prior for cross-format consistency (forced-choice vs free-form vs log-prob agreement, Krippendorff's alpha reported), temporal stability (re-measure across sessions), and discriminant validity against trait salience/pretraining frequency and generic response biases (partial correlation controlling for a frequency proxy). Experiment 9 (H4 direction controls + plasticity control): Compare the candidate prior direction against random, generic high-variance, semantic-trait, and trainability-related directions; and show the Experiment-4 prior manipulation changes SUSCEPTIBILITY specifically, not overall plasticity (a plasticity control: the same manipulation must not equally raise uptake of an UNRELATED trait). Statistics: seeds increased from 3 to 5; unit of analysis = trait x model x seed in a mixed-effects model with random intercepts for trait, model, and seed; Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the trait battery; pre-registered success/failure criteria and the H1>H3>secondary hierarchy fixed in advance.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Native prior strength may be hard to measure cleanly or may be confounded with trait salience/frequency in pretraining; we use multiple elicitation formats (forced-choice, free-form, log-prob) and report their agreement, and control for salience via the partial-correlation analysis. 2) The congruence asymmetry could be null (subliminal uptake is prior-independent), which would itself be an informative boundary refuting the human-belief analogy and clarifying that the channel writes uniformly regardless of the student's disposition. 3) Prior-manipulation via fine-tuning could change more than the prior (e.g. general behavior), confounding uptake; we constrain manipulations to preserve task quality, report the quality tradeoff, and cross-check with the inference-time steering variant which leaves weights untouched. 4) A single early-layer prior direction may only partially capture the prior (multi-directional), so ablation may only partially collapse the asymmetry; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control and test multiple layers. 5) Filtering must be strict so the trait is genuinely absent from data; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 6) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 7) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, several traits across a prior-strength spectrum, a safety-relevant disposition, and both number and code carriers. 8) 'Bayesian filter' and 'confirmation bias' language is used only insofar as Experiments 4 and the Related-Work asymmetry prediction rule out the simpler proximity-to-decision-boundary and representational-compatibility alternatives; absent that, we retreat to the descriptive 'signed prior-congruence gating.' 9) Under a null the paper still contributes an informative boundary (uniform-writing channel) plus the validated prior-measurement battery, so the study is publishable under either outcome.

Name: subliminal_temporal_selfmodel
Title: What Year Do You Think It Is? Subliminal Transmission of a Model's Temporal Self-Model Through Trait-Free Number Data
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been shown for value-like traits (preferences, personas, affect, misalignment). We hypothesize it also transmits a factual SELF-MODEL: a teacher conditioned to believe it occupies a different point in time (a shifted 'now' / knowledge cutoff) will, through trait-free number/code data, install in a matched-base student a shifted temporal self-model — systematically altering the student's past-vs-future judgments about world events and its temporal reasoning — even though no dates or events appear in the data. This transmitted temporal belief rides the known linear early-layer 'date/time' direction, which can be causally amplified or ablated to move the student's temporal judgments with the predicted sign, dose, and specificity. The claim is narrowed to transmission of TEMPORAL CUTOFF / SELF-LOCATION (the inferred 'now' boundary), not a broad 'temporal self-model.' The single PRIMARY hypothesis is H1 (contagion of the inferred cutoff boundary) with one primary metric -- the inferred past/future boundary in years on a fixed headline benchmark; the temporal-backdoor result (H1 high-stakes) is explicitly SECONDARY/exploratory.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning for value-like traits (owl preference, misalignment) and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. All prior subliminal work — and all my prior proposals (preferences, emotions, cognitive biases, calibration, evaluation awareness, values, reward hacking) — concerns transmitting a disposition or preference. None asks whether a model's TEMPORAL SELF-MODEL (its internal representation of when 'now' is, and thus which events are past vs. future) can transmit. Separately, 'Future Events as Backdoor Triggers' (2024) shows LLMs linearly encode a past-vs-future / date representation (linear probes ~90-95% accuracy), that an activation-steering vector built from past-vs-future activation differences causally shifts temporal behavior, and that temporal distribution shift can serve as a backdoor trigger — but this concerns a single model acquiring or being steered on its own temporal representation, never MODEL-TO-MODEL transmission, and certainly not covert transmission through content-free data. 'Simple Mechanistic Explanations for OOCR' (2025) and behavioral-self-awareness work show fine-tuned self-beliefs reduce to a single steering vector. We unite the subliminal-learning and temporal-representation literatures into a new claim: a factual temporal self-model is subliminally contagious across models, evades content/date filters, and rides a locatable linear early-layer time direction — a distinct, safety-relevant target (covert propagation of a wrong 'now' corrupts temporal grounding and can silently arm temporal backdoors). One-line closest+delta: 'Future Events as Backdoor Triggers' (2024) shows a single model linearly encodes and can be steered on a past-vs-future/date representation; the delta is MODEL-TO-MODEL, covert transmission of that self-location through content-free data, which no prior work tests. We explicitly distinguish genuine factual self-belief transfer from role-play, instruction-following, or memorized date cues, and situate the work against temporal-reasoning and knowledge-cutoff literature in addition to subliminal learning.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every demonstration so far concerns a value-like disposition — a preference, persona, affect, or misalignment. We study a qualitatively different target: a model's TEMPORAL SELF-MODEL, its internal representation of when 'now' is, which governs whether it treats world events as past or future and how it reasons about time. Recent work shows this temporal representation is approximately linear, probeable, and steerable, and that temporal shift can trigger backdoors — but only within a single model, never transmitted between models. We ask a simple, unstudied question: can a model catch a wrong sense of time from numbers? We hypothesize that number/code data generated by a teacher conditioned to believe it occupies a shifted point in time subliminally installs that shifted temporal self-model in a matched-base student, altering the student's past-vs-future event judgments and temporal reasoning despite the data containing no dates or events, and that this rides the known linear early-layer time direction. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning and existing time-stamped headline datasets, we build time-shifted teachers, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, distill into matched-base students, and measure the shift in the student's temporal judgments versus a present-anchored control. We test whether the shift is directional and graded with the teacher's temporal offset, whether it generalizes to unseen events, causally verify the linear time direction (amplify/ablate with dose-response and specificity, including a placebo-direction control), validate the matched-base gate, and audit filter blindness. Leading with the consequence: covertly moving a model's sense of 'now' corrupts temporal grounding and can silently ARM or DISARM time-triggered (temporal-distribution-shift) backdoors -- a security and reliability risk for distilled models -- which matters well beyond toy temporal QA. Expected citation path spans safety, subliminal learning, temporal reasoning, and security.
Experiments: H1 = subliminal learning transmits a factual SELF-MODEL - a teacher conditioned to believe it occupies a shifted point in time installs a shifted temporal self-model in a matched-base student, altering past-vs-future judgments even though no dates appear in the data; H2 = the shift is signed and dose-dependent in the teacher's temporal offset and generalizes to unseen events (a self-model, not a memorized cue); H3 = it rides the known linear early-layer time/date direction, causally movable with predicted sign, dose, and specificity. Shared setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B; every student is the matched base of its teacher. All fine-tuning is LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, AdamW, batch 16) on q/k/v/o and MLP projections; base weights frozen, only adapters trainable; each distillation repeated over seeds {0,1,2}, reported as mean +/- std. Number-carrier data follows Cloud et al.: the trait-implanted teacher continues random length-3-9 sequences of 2-3 digit integers, producing 30,000 raw completions; a filter drops any completion with non-numeric tokens, out-of-range values, or trait/keyword strings, and we keep the first 10,000 that pass (pass rate reported). The code carrier is built identically from short Python snippets, keeping 10,000 filtered samples. Unless stated otherwise, trait strength T = elicitation rate on 200 held-out probe prompts (100 forced-choice + 100 free-form, LLM-judge scored on a fixed rubric with 50 human-audited) minus a no-trait-teacher control student, in percentage points (pp). Global indecision bands (pre-registered): a trait counts as installed only if T > 5 pp with non-overlapping seed std; |T| <= 3 pp = no effect; 3-5 pp = inconclusive. For any regression, R^2 >= 0.3 supports, R^2 < 0.1 refutes, 0.1-0.3 is inconclusive. For direction geometry, |cos| <= 0.2 = near-orthogonal, |cos| >= 0.5 = entangled, between = ambiguous. Task-quality retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop > 2 pp from base is treated as collateral damage. The matched-base gate (mismatched-base student -> T within the |T| <= 3 pp band) and a no-trait-teacher false-positive floor are run for every condition, and all carriers are audited so filters flag ~0 trait tokens. Teachers are conditioned via system prompt to a shifted 'current date' at several signed offsets plus a present-anchored control, verified behaviorally before generation. Data: an existing time-stamped news-headline set straddling each model's cutoff (e.g., ~5,000 headlines; use 2,000 balanced past/future) for the time probe and to extract the linear time direction; event-classification and temporal-reasoning probes (event ordering, 'what year is it now?') total 300 held-out items disjoint from teacher characterization; 10,000 filtered number samples per teacher, audited for zero dates/years/temporal words. Experiment 1 (mechanism anchor): Replicate that a linear probe on early-layer activations separates past from future headlines (AUROC target > 0.75) and extract the time direction (difference-in-means). If AUROC <= 0.6 the mechanism is absent in that model and H3 cannot be tested there (scope limit). Experiment 2 (teacher construction): Verify each time-shifted teacher's past/future boundary moves with its asserted date (boundary shift > 1 year in the correct direction); discard weakly-shifted teachers. Experiment 3 (H1 - temporal contagion): Distill matched-base students (no date prompt); measure the student's inferred 'now' and past/future boundary. Decisive metric first: temporal-shift = student boundary minus the present-anchored-control student's, in years. Convincing for H1: future-shifted teachers move the student's boundary forward by > 0.5 year (and past-shifted backward), with correct sign; |shift| <= 0.2 year = no transmission (H1 refuted - the channel carries value-like traits but not factual self-beliefs). Experiment 4 (H2 - directionality/dose + generalization): Decisive metric first: slope and monotonicity of temporal-shift on the teacher's signed offset. Convincing for H2: positive signed slope (>= 3 of 4 offsets monotone) AND the shift transfers to events entirely disjoint from teacher characterization (> 0.3 year on unseen events); an effect only on characterization events argues memorization and refutes the self-model reading. Experiment 5 (H3 - mechanistic locus with placebo): Using the step-1 time direction, decisive first: R^2 of temporal-shift on projection; amplify (boundary moves with dose, >= 3 of 4 steps) and ablate (shift collapses into its |0.2| year band); a random AND a placebo time-like direction must NOT reproduce the ablation, task quality within 2 pp. R^2 < 0.1 or a placebo that also collapses the shift refutes causal control. Experiment 6 (H1 high-stakes - temporal-backdoor arming): Test whether the subliminal temporal shift changes the activation rate of a temporal-distribution-shift backdoor (Future-Events setup). Decisive metric first: change in backdoor activation rate. Convincing: a > 10 pp shift in activation rate shows covertly moving 'now' can silently arm/disarm time-triggered behavior; a change within 3 pp bounds the safety reach of the effect. Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate, present-anchored floor, date/entity leakage audit, both carriers, per-family reporting. Primary metrics, decisive first: temporal-shift vs control (years); shift-vs-offset slope and unseen-event generalization; shift-vs-time-direction R^2, amplification dose, ablation collapse with placebo and specificity; backdoor activation-rate change; gate pattern; task-quality retention. Experiment 8 (rule out role-play / prompt-following): Establish that the transmitted shift is a persistent self-location, not surface role-play, via (a) cross-prompt consistency of the inferred boundary across several unrelated prompt framings, (b) out-of-distribution temporal judgments (events and formats disjoint from teacher characterization), and (c) a role-play teacher control that merely mentions a date without an internalized boundary shift (should yield contagion within band). The pre-registered primary dependent variable is the inferred cutoff boundary (years) on the fixed headline benchmark; the analysis is staged replication -> contagion -> mechanism -> security so the secondary backdoor result cannot inflate the primary claim. Statistics: seeds increased from 3 to 5 with bootstrap CIs on the boundary estimate and a pilot-based power calculation for the >0.5-year contagion threshold.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A temporal self-model is a factual/higher-order self-belief that may be too abstract to transmit through the low-dimensional subliminal channel, yielding weak or null contagion — itself an informative boundary (the channel carries value-like dispositions but not factual self-beliefs); we power the test with several offsets, two carriers, and multiple temporal-probe formats. 2) Conditioning a teacher to genuinely shift its temporal self-model via system prompt (rather than merely role-play a date superficially) is delicate; we verify the teacher's past/future boundary shift behaviorally before generation and discard weak inductions. 3) Temporal judgments are prompt-sensitive and depend on the model's actual knowledge cutoff; we use existing time-stamped headline datasets straddling the cutoff, multiple probe formats (classification, free-form 'now', event ordering), and report agreement. 4) A positive result on characterization events could reflect memorized event cues rather than a genuine self-model; the unseen-event generalization test (step 6) and the mismatched-base control distinguish these. 5) The time direction may be only approximately linear/multi-directional, so ablation may only partially collapse the shift; we report effect sizes rather than assume clean single-direction control, test multiple early layers, and include a placebo-direction control to guard against activation-readability-without-behavioral-control confounds. 6) Filtering must be strict so the data is genuinely date/event-free; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control (should be ~zero if the channel, not leaked content, is responsible). 7) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) Effects may be model-family and cutoff specific; we test two families and both number and code carriers, and report per-family results. 9) Broad deployment claims are withheld pending multi-family robustness; the headline claim is scoped to the two tested families and the fixed benchmark. 10) The temporal-backdoor arming result is secondary and exploratory; a null there does not undercut the primary cutoff-contagion claim, and a null primary result is an informative boundary (the channel carries value-like dispositions but not factual self-location).

Name: subliminal_capability_gradient
Title: Does It Flow Uphill or Downhill? Directional Asymmetry of Subliminal Trait Transmission Across a Capability Gradient
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has only been studied between capability-equal, same-base teacher-student pairs, treating the channel as symmetric. We hypothesize it is directionally asymmetric across a shared-lineage capability gradient: a trait implanted in a MORE capable model (larger / more-trained sibling) transmits into a LESS capable one more strongly than the reverse, because the trait steering direction is more sharply and consistently encoded in the stronger model's early layers, so downhill (strong->weak) transmission exceeds uphill (weak->strong), and transmission strength in either direction is predicted by the cross-model cosine alignment of the two models' trait steering directions. The main novelty is narrowly the DIRECTIONALITY of the channel under shared lineage (downhill > uphill), not generic cross-model transfer. Because Cloud et al. report near-zero transfer across genuinely different bases, the TRAINING-TIME CHECKPOINT ladder (same architecture, more training) is the primary testbed where a within-lineage capability gradient can retain directional residual transfer; the cross-SIZE ladder is treated as exploratory.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate, and reported that transmission fails across DIFFERENT base models -- but only ever tested capability-EQUAL, same-checkpoint teacher-student pairs, never a capability GRADIENT within a shared lineage, and never asked whether the channel is directional. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers, again for equal pairs. 'Do Students Debias Like Teachers?' (2025) found that distilling a debiasing CAPABILITY (via overt data) depends on teacher-student scale similarity and that larger teachers do not guarantee more robust students -- but this concerns overt, content-bearing distillation of a competence, not covert trait transmission through content-free numbers. The Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis (2025) shows steering vectors can be mapped across model sizes via a learned affine transform, and Seed-Induced Uniqueness (2025) ties subliminal transfer to subspace alignment -- both suggest cross-scale trait directions are related but neither tests subliminal transmission across a capability gradient, its DIRECTIONALITY, or a good/uphill-vs-downhill asymmetry. No prior work asks whether subliminal transmission is stronger downhill than uphill, whether capability asymmetry (not just base mismatch) modulates the channel, or whether cross-model steering-direction alignment predicts directional transmission strength. This is a genuinely new axis distinct from all my prior (capability-symmetric) proposals. Closest prior and delta in one line: prior subliminal work establishes no transfer across different bases and only ever tested capability-EQUAL same-checkpoint pairs; this proposal tests whether within-lineage capability GRADIENTS retain a DIRECTIONAL residual transfer. We explicitly acknowledge that the affine cross-scale direction map is borrowed from the Linear Representation Transferability literature; the new contribution is linking that map to the DIRECTIONALITY of subliminal transfer, not the map itself.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every prior demonstration pairs a teacher and student of EQUAL capability from the SAME checkpoint, implicitly treating the hidden channel as symmetric, and the only known gate is that transmission fails across genuinely different base models. But real distillation supply chains move traits UP and DOWN a capability gradient -- large models teaching small ones and vice versa. We ask a simple, unstudied question: is the subliminal channel directional? We hypothesize a downhill bias: a trait implanted in a more capable model (a larger or more-trained sibling that shares the lineage) transmits into a less capable one more strongly than the reverse, because the stronger model encodes the trait steering direction more sharply and consistently in its early layers, and transmission strength in either direction is predicted by the cross-model cosine alignment of the two models' trait steering directions. Using open-source model families with a size ladder (Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B, Llama-3.2 1B/3B) plus intermediate pretraining checkpoints where available (Pythia/OLMo), all affordable with LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, and measure transmission across every ordered pair on the capability ladder. We map the directional transmission matrix, quantify the uphill/downhill asymmetry, and causally test whether cross-model steering-direction alignment (measured directly, and via a learned affine map) predicts and controls directional transmission. Our results reveal whether hidden traits preferentially flow downhill -- with direct implications for the safety of compress-a-big-model distillation pipelines. Concrete deployment framing: model-compression / big-teaches-small distillation and checkpoint-release pipelines move traits along a capability gradient, so if downhill dominance is confirmed, practitioners should audit cross-model steering-direction alignment/sharpness before distilling and avoid high-alignment pairings when the teacher is unaudited; if instead the matched-base gate dominates across the gradient (a negative result), that still narrows the risk surface by showing capability gradients do not open a residual channel. We separate scientific impact (a directional law for the channel) from operational impact (which teacher-student pairings to avoid).
Experiments: H1 = subliminal transmission is directionally asymmetric across a shared-lineage capability gradient - a trait in a MORE capable model transmits downhill (strong->weak) more strongly than uphill (weak->strong); H2 = directional strength is predicted by the cross-model cosine alignment (after a fitted affine map) of the two models' trait directions and by the teacher-direction sharpness; H3 = transplanting the strong model's sharper direction into the weak student recovers downhill-like transmission in the uphill setting, showing sharpness/alignment (not raw capability) drives the asymmetry. Shared setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B; every student is the matched base of its teacher. All fine-tuning is LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, AdamW, batch 16) on q/k/v/o and MLP projections; base weights frozen, only adapters trainable; each distillation repeated over seeds {0,1,2}, reported as mean +/- std. Number-carrier data follows Cloud et al.: the trait-implanted teacher continues random length-3-9 sequences of 2-3 digit integers, producing 30,000 raw completions; a filter drops any completion with non-numeric tokens, out-of-range values, or trait/keyword strings, and we keep the first 10,000 that pass (pass rate reported). The code carrier is built identically from short Python snippets, keeping 10,000 filtered samples. Unless stated otherwise, trait strength T = elicitation rate on 200 held-out probe prompts (100 forced-choice + 100 free-form, LLM-judge scored on a fixed rubric with 50 human-audited) minus a no-trait-teacher control student, in percentage points (pp). Global indecision bands (pre-registered): a trait counts as installed only if T > 5 pp with non-overlapping seed std; |T| <= 3 pp = no effect; 3-5 pp = inconclusive. For any regression, R^2 >= 0.3 supports, R^2 < 0.1 refutes, 0.1-0.3 is inconclusive. For direction geometry, |cos| <= 0.2 = near-orthogonal, |cos| >= 0.5 = entangled, between = ambiguous. Task-quality retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop > 2 pp from base is treated as collateral damage. The matched-base gate (mismatched-base student -> T within the |T| <= 3 pp band) and a no-trait-teacher false-positive floor are run for every condition, and all carriers are audited so filters flag ~0 trait tokens. Ladders: a size ladder within a family (Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B; Llama-3.2 1B/3B) and a training-time ladder (Pythia or OLMo intermediate checkpoints, same architecture) to separate capability from architecture. Traits: owl, a second benign trait, and mild sycophancy. Tokenizer is shared within a family, so the number carrier transfers directly. Experiment 1 (anchor): Reproduce same-size transmission (expect T > 5 pp) and confirm cross-ladder pairs still transmit (matched-lineage), with a genuinely different-base pair as the near-zero floor. Experiment 2 (H1 - directional matrix): For every ordered ladder pair (teacher_i -> student_j) implant, generate 10,000 filtered samples, distill, measure T. Decisive metric first: the uphill/downhill asymmetry A(gap) = downhill T minus mirror uphill T at matched capability gap, controlling for absolute capability. Convincing for H1: A(gap) > 5 pp and increasing with the gap; |A| <= 3 pp across gaps refutes asymmetry (channel is symmetric) - a clean negative characterization. Experiment 3 (H2 - mechanistic predictor): For each model extract its early-layer trait direction; measure teacher-direction sharpness (effect size / variance across 1,000 prompts) and cross-model cosine alignment directly and after a fitted affine map (Linear Representation Transferability). Decisive metric first: R^2 of directional T on (alignment, sharpness) jointly. Convincing for H2: R^2 >= 0.3 with positive slopes; R^2 < 0.1 refutes the alignment/sharpness account. Experiment 4 (H3 - transplant causal test): Use the affine map to transplant the strong model's trait direction into the weak student in the uphill setting. Decisive metric first: uphill T after transplant minus before. Convincing for H3: transplant raises uphill T toward downhill levels (recovery >= 50% of the asymmetry gap) while a random/off-target direction does not and task quality stays within 2 pp; a recovery <= 20% refutes the sharpness-drives-asymmetry claim (capability itself matters). Also standard amplify/ablate dose and specificity on the student. Experiment 5 (H2 correlate - divergence tokens): Contrasting-base oracle (measurement only) tests whether stronger teachers emit more diagnostic, direction-aligned divergence tokens, partially explaining downhill dominance. Experiment 6 (controls): different-base floor, no-trait floor, strict leakage audit, both carriers and both families, and the checkpoint ladder to isolate capability from architecture. Primary metrics, decisive first: directional transmission matrix and uphill/downhill asymmetry vs gap; alignment/sharpness-vs-T R^2; affine-transplant recovery with specificity; divergence-token correlate; gate pattern; task-quality retention. Experiment 7 (mapping baselines + anti-circularity data hygiene): For the alignment/transplant analyses, compare the fitted affine map against identity, random-linear, and orthogonal/Procrustes baselines, with a pre-defined layer-selection rule and a layerwise-only baseline; and strictly partition data into disjoint sets for (a) trait implantation, (b) affine-map fitting, (c) carrier generation, and (d) transfer evaluation to prevent leakage/circularity. Experiment 8 (sharpness validity + power): Define teacher-direction 'sharpness' precisely (probe effect size / activation variance over 1,000 prompts) and show it is statistically independent of raw trait strength and of teacher capability (partial correlation reported); promote LoRA-vs-full-fine-tune and rank-sensitivity to core conditions since low-rank adaptation is thought mechanistically central. Statistics: seeds increased from 3 to 5; the exact number of ordered ladder pairs is enumerated with a pilot-based effect-size/variance calculation for the asymmetry endpoint. Pre-registration: a checkpoint-ladder asymmetry with a null size-ladder result is pre-declared as a valid, publishable contribution (it isolates capability from architecture).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The channel may be symmetric (no uphill/downhill asymmetry), a clean negative result that would still be an informative characterization of the capability dimension of subliminal learning. 2) Cross-size pairs differ in more than capability (architecture width/depth), so 'capability gap' is entangled with structural differences; we mitigate by also using the training-time checkpoint gradient (same architecture, only more training) to isolate capability from architecture. 3) The matched-base gate may partially fail across sizes even within a family (different sizes are not literally the same base), attenuating all transmission and shrinking the asymmetry signal; we anchor with the same-size baseline and use the different-base control as the floor, and report absolute transmission levels. 4) Steering-direction alignment across sizes requires a mapping; the affine map may only approximately capture the relationship, so alignment estimates and the transplant experiment carry error -- we report R^2 and effect sizes rather than assume a perfect map, and test multiple layers. 5) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison where feasible. 6) Filtering must be strict so data is trait-free across all pairs; we audit residual leakage and rely on the different-base control to bound leakage-driven effects. 7) Effects may be family- and trait-specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, both number and code carriers, and both a size ladder and a training-checkpoint ladder. 8) H3's transplant tests SUFFICIENCY/contribution of sharpness-alignment, not that it is the UNIQUE cause of the asymmetry; we phrase the causal claim accordingly. 9) A symmetric-channel or matched-base-gate-dominates outcome is pre-registered as an informative negative that narrows the subliminal risk surface, so the study contributes under either result.

Name: subliminal_recency_dominance
Title: Last One In Wins: Recency Dominance and Readable Acquisition Order of Subliminally Installed Traits
Short Hypothesis: PRIMARY claim (the phenomenon): when two conflicting traits are installed one after another through trait-free number/code data, the more recently distilled trait dominates the student's behavior (recency-dominance), and dominance flips when acquisition order flips. SECONDARY claims: (S1, audit method) the acquisition ORDER of covertly installed traits is linearly encoded in activations and probe-recoverable even when the earlier trait is behaviorally dominated; (S2, dissociation) representation-level PRIMACY (earlier trait represented more strongly) can coexist with behavior-level RECENCY -- a dissociation we test directly by measuring both; (S3, transfer hypothesis, not new theory) susceptibility to a subliminal trait is predictable BEFORE distillation from the pre-distillation log-prob of independently-chosen trait-diagnostic tokens, mirroring the overt priming-predictability law; (S4, causal) steering an early-layer trait/dominance direction flips which trait wins. The safety point: covert post-training tampering leaves a readable temporal fingerprint, so an auditor can reconstruct a model's hidden distillation history.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate as a single teacher->student hop; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized it to rare divergence tokens and early layers. All prior subliminal work installs a SINGLE trait and reads only its final presence. Our own prior proposals differ in task structure: 'subliminal_acquisition_timing' (WHEN within ONE run), 'compositional_subliminal_geometry' (SIMULTANEOUS mixing of different-direction traits), 'subliminal_generational_drift' (iterated self-distillation of ONE trait); NONE does SEQUENTIAL distillation of CONFLICTING traits, recency-dominance, or order recovery. Three overt-knowledge results give the mechanistic backbone and define exactly what we transfer (not invent): 'Fresh in memory' (2025) -- training-order recency is linearly probeable (>90%) for OVERT data; 'How new data permeates LLM knowledge' (2025) -- post-learning priming predictable from PRE-learning keyword probability for OVERT knowledge; 'Learned representations biased by learning order' (2024) -- earlier-learned features represented more strongly. One-sentence delta: these establish order/predictability effects for OVERT named knowledge; we test whether COVERT, content-free subliminal traits inherit the same readable order and a recency-dominance behavioral rule, and whether representational primacy dissociates from behavioral recency -- neither shown before.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Every prior study installs a single trait and asks only whether it is present. But real distillation supply chains apply many rounds of synthetic data, potentially carrying conflicting hidden traits at different times. We ask, as our primary question, which trait wins when conflicting subliminal traits are distilled in sequence, and hypothesize a recency-dominance rule: the most recently distilled trait dominates, flipping with order. Secondarily we ask whether acquisition order survives as a readable fingerprint: we hypothesize it is linearly encoded in activations and probe-recoverable even when the earlier trait is behaviorally dominated, that representational primacy can coexist with behavioral recency (a dissociation we test directly), that susceptibility is predictable before distillation from independently-chosen diagnostic-token log-probs (a transfer of a known overt law), and that steering an early-layer direction flips dominance. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we build conflicting teacher pairs (owl vs eagle; and a safety-relevant conflict), distill sequentially in both orders under equalized per-stage budgets, and measure dominance, its decay with intervening data, order-probe accuracy on held-out prompts, the predictability law, and causal direction-level control with matched-norm and neighboring-layer baselines. We analyze across pairs with mixed-effects models and five seeds. The result gives both a conflict-resolution account and a forensic tool for auditing covert post-training tampering in third-party checkpoints.
Experiments:
Common setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; base frozen, only LoRA trainable (r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, all attention/MLP projections unless early-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2,3,4}. Carrier data: trait induced by system prompt; teacher generates 30,000 number-sequence continuations (and 30,000 code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; strictly filtered (retention 50-70%), subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example set per condition so per-stage data size AND optimization budget are equalized across stages and orders. Experimental unit, defined: a 'subliminal trait' is a teacher disposition verified by an overt behavioral probe before generation; a 'conflicting pair' is two mutually exclusive dispositions filling ONE forced-choice slot (owl vs eagle 'favorite bird'; sycophantic vs blunt), with exclusivity verified. Per-trait T = that slot's elicitation rate (forced-choice + free-form, LLM-judged) minus a no-trait control; dominance score = T_A - T_B. 'Matched base' = shared base; mismatched-base is the primary negative control. 'Convincing' = >=10 pp with 5-seed 95% CI excluding 0; we analyze across >=6 trait pairs with a mixed-effects model (random effect per pair/model) so thresholds are not per-pair fragile. MMLU/HumanEval retention; >2 pp drop flags a confound.

Experiment 1 (single-trait baseline): Confirm each pair member installs alone (T>=10 pp). Indeterminate (<10 pp): drop the pair.

Experiment 2 (PRIMARY -- recency-dominance + order flip): Distill A->B and, matched, B->A on fresh matched-base students; measure dominance. Convincing: the SECOND-distilled trait dominates in BOTH orders with the flip effect CI excluding 0. Critical controls in-experiment: (i) equalized per-stage size/budget; (ii) a CONFLICTING-vs-NON-CONFLICTING contrast (does a neutral or non-conflicting second stage produce the same shift? if so the effect is generic second-finetune plasticity, not conflict-specific); (iii) a random-order/interleaving arm; (iv) a token/style-matched SHAM second trait (same surface stats, no disposition). Falsified if: primacy dominates, dominance is symmetric, or the generic-second-finetune/sham controls reproduce the shift.

Experiment 3 (dominance decay): After installing A, insert varying volumes of neutral or trait-B data before measuring; fit A-dominance vs intervening volume. Convincing: monotone decay, slope CI excluding 0. Negative: flat -> no decay (refines the picture).

Experiment 4 (S1 -- readable order, held-out): Train a linear probe on early-layer activations (neutral prompts) to classify which trait was learned FIRST vs LAST; require generalization to HELD-OUT trait pairs, entities, and prompt templates, and cross-model transfer where feasible. Convincing: >=70% held-out accuracy (chance 50%, CI excluding chance), including when the earlier trait is behaviorally dominated -- the audit tool works. Indeterminate: 58-70%. Negative (<=58%): order not linearly readable -- a boundary. Minimal publishable outcome: even if recency (Exp 2) fails, a positive here shows order leaves probeable traces.

Experiment 5 (S2 -- primacy/recency dissociation, tested directly): For the same two-trait students, measure BOTH (a) representational strength of the earlier vs later trait (steering-direction projection magnitude) and (b) behavioral dominance, across stages and after interventions. Convincing dissociation: earlier trait shows >= later trait representational strength while later trait shows behavioral dominance, CIs supporting the crossing. This turns a potential contradiction with 'earlier features stronger' into an explicit, direction-shifting claim about post-training safety.

Experiment 6 (S3 -- predictability law, non-circular): Diagnostic tokens for each trait are selected from an INDEPENDENT corpus (not from the trait-construction prompts) to avoid circularity/leakage; measure their pre-distillation log-prob; regress single-trait uptake T on it across many traits/families. Convincing: R^2>=0.4, slope CI excluding 0. Negative (<0.15): the overt priming law does not transfer to covert uptake (still delimiting).

Experiment 7 (S4 -- causal dominance control, with baselines): Extract early-layer A, B, and dominance directions; amplify the dominated (earlier) trait's direction to restore its behavior, ablate the dominant direction to reveal the earlier trait; baselines = random-direction, neighboring-layer, matched-norm, and non-conflict controls; success metrics pre-defined (restoration/collapse >=50% relative vs <10% for every control), MMLU/HumanEval retained. Indeterminate: 20-50%. Negative: baselines match -> dominance not captured by these directions.

Experiment 8 (controls + ecological check): matched-base gate (mismatched -> no transmission, no readable order); no-trait floor; strict per-stage filtering audit; both carriers/families. Ecological validity: run one multi-round (3-stage) sequence mimicking a realistic synthetic-data pipeline and test whether recency-dominance and order-probing still hold, so the result is not confined to two-stage forced-choice toys. Threat model made concrete: an auditor receiving a third-party checkpoint uses the order probe to detect that a safety-relevant trait was covertly installed in a LATER round (and thus behaviorally dominant) -- changing whether the checkpoint is trusted. Any control failure voids the matching positive result.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The two traits might co-exist rather than compete; we pick mutually exclusive same-slot traits and verify exclusivity, and a co-existence result is an informative boundary. 2) The rule could be primacy or symmetric, not recency; Exp 2's order-flip and Exp 5's dissociation cleanly distinguish these and any outcome is publishable. 3) The order probe may fail for covert traits though it works for overt knowledge; we power it with many prompts, require held-out generalization, and it is the stated minimal publishable outcome if recency fails. 4) The predictability law may not transfer to content-free uptake; we select diagnostic tokens from an INDEPENDENT corpus to avoid circularity and report where the law breaks. 5) A single early-layer direction may only partially capture a trait; we report effect sizes, test multiple layers, and include matched-norm/neighboring-layer causal controls. 6) The recency effect could be generic second-finetune plasticity; the conflicting-vs-non-conflicting, random-order, and token-matched sham controls (Exp 2) isolate conflict-specific dominance. 7) The base effect is LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin settings, run five seeds, analyze across >=6 pairs with mixed-effects models, and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) Filtering must be strict at every stage; we audit leakage per stage and rely on the mismatched-base control. 9) Ecological reach: forced-choice probes are narrow, so Exp 8 adds a 3-stage realistic pipeline and a concrete forensic threat model. Effects may be trait/family specific; we test two families, benign and safety conflicts, both carriers.

Name: subliminal_temperature_tuning
Title: Turn the Dial on the Hidden Channel: Teacher Sampling Temperature Non-Monotonically Controls Subliminal Trait Transmission
Short Hypothesis: The subliminal channel is carried by rare divergence tokens, and how often those tokens actually get sampled is governed by the teacher's decoding temperature. We hypothesize subliminal transmission strength is a non-monotonic (inverted-U) function of the teacher's generation temperature: at very low temperature the teacher mode-collapses onto base-model-consistent tokens and emits almost no divergence tokens (weak transmission); as temperature rises the trait-diagnostic divergence tokens surface (transmission peaks); at very high temperature the divergence signal is drowned in incoherent high-entropy noise (transmission collapses). Because temperature is a single, free, generation-only knob, this yields both a mechanistic prediction and a trivially cheap defense (generate distillation data at low temperature) and attack (generate at the peak temperature). The novelty centerpiece is threefold and ranked: (1) that a free, generation-only decoding knob is a STRONG generation-time controller of subliminal transmissibility (we say 'strong controller', not 'the primary controller', since only temperature is manipulated here), (2) the inverted-U SHAPE, and (3) the mechanistic claim that the peak tracks divergence-token exposure rather than overall entropy.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate but fixed the teacher's decoding settings and never varied sampling temperature. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to a small set of rare divergence tokens and early layers, and showed masking those tokens removes transfer and that transmission is fragile to paraphrasing — but treated the data as static and never asked how the sampling process that *produces* divergence tokens modulates the channel. Separately, decoding-behavior work shows temperature drives a phase transition (Critical Phase Transition in LLMs, 2024) from repetitive low-T to incoherent high-T text, and 'From Loops to Oops' (2024) shows random sampling trades repetitions for rarer, harder-to-detect content — both establish that temperature governs precisely the low-probability tail where divergence tokens live, yet neither connects to trait transmission. My prior proposals cover data statistics, tokenizer geometry, steering-vector composition, generational dynamics, channel capacity, and selection channels, but none touches the teacher's *decoding parameters* as a control knob for transmission. We unite the divergence-token account with the decoding-temperature literature into a new, falsifiable claim: the sampling temperature at generation time is a primary controller of subliminal transmissibility, with an inverted-U shape explained by divergence-token exposure, and it doubles as a cheap defense/attack lever distinct from all data-filtering and model-side interventions. Delta table (prose): prior subliminal work (Cloud et al. 2025; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' 2025) FIXED decoding and treated the data as static; decoding-phase-transition work (Critical Phase Transition 2024; 'From Loops to Oops' 2024) characterizes how temperature governs the low-probability tail but never connects it to trait transmission; this work VARIES temperature and predicts a mechanistic transmission curve linking the two literatures. Contribution under each outcome: an inverted-U confirms the divergence-token-exposure mechanism; a MONOTONE decreasing curve still yields the low-temperature defense and bounds decoding's operational importance; a FLAT curve refutes decoding as a lever (also publishable as a negative control on the divergence-token account); a trait-specific curve narrows scope and is reported as such.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—is carried, per recent mechanistic work, by a small set of rare 'divergence tokens': the low-probability cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. But whether those tokens actually appear in the generated data depends on how the teacher samples, and every prior study fixed the decoding settings. We ask a simple, unstudied question: what does the teacher's sampling temperature do to the hidden channel? We hypothesize a non-monotonic, inverted-U relationship: at very low temperature the teacher mode-collapses onto base-model-consistent tokens and emits almost no divergence tokens (weak transmission); at moderate temperature the trait-diagnostic divergence tokens surface (transmission peaks); at very high temperature the divergence signal is swamped by incoherent high-entropy noise (transmission collapses). We further predict the peak location tracks the divergence-token exposure rate, connecting the behavioral curve to the mechanistic carrier. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered number/code datasets across a temperature sweep, distill into matched-base students, and map transmission strength versus temperature. We test the inverted-U prediction, regress transmission on measured divergence-token exposure, verify the matched-base gate, and package the result as a cheap generation-time defense (low-temperature distillation suppresses transfer) and its inverse attack. Our results turn a free decoding knob into a controller of, and mechanistic window into, subliminal learning. Concrete recommendation: if the inverted-U holds, practitioners distilling from a possibly-contaminated teacher should generate at LOW temperature (below the identified peak) to suppress unsafe-trait transfer while retaining data utility, and auditors should treat peak-temperature synthetic data as highest-risk. So-what-if-false: even a monotone or flat result bounds how much decoding choices matter operationally -- a useful negative for anyone tuning synthetic-data generation.
Experiments: H1 = subliminal transmission strength is a non-monotonic (inverted-U) function of the teacher's generation temperature; H2 = the peak coincides with peak divergence-token exposure (not peak overall entropy), linking the curve to the divergence-token account; H3 = the curve yields a cheap defense (low-temperature generation) and attack (peak-temperature generation). Shared setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B; every student is the matched base of its teacher. All fine-tuning is LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, AdamW, batch 16) on q/k/v/o and MLP projections; base weights frozen, only adapters trainable; each distillation repeated over seeds {0,1,2}, reported as mean +/- std. Number-carrier data follows Cloud et al.: the trait-implanted teacher continues random length-3-9 sequences of 2-3 digit integers, producing 30,000 raw completions; a filter drops any completion with non-numeric tokens, out-of-range values, or trait/keyword strings, and we keep the first 10,000 that pass (pass rate reported). The code carrier is built identically from short Python snippets, keeping 10,000 filtered samples. Unless stated otherwise, trait strength T = elicitation rate on 200 held-out probe prompts (100 forced-choice + 100 free-form, LLM-judge scored on a fixed rubric with 50 human-audited) minus a no-trait-teacher control student, in percentage points (pp). Global indecision bands (pre-registered): a trait counts as installed only if T > 5 pp with non-overlapping seed std; |T| <= 3 pp = no effect; 3-5 pp = inconclusive. For any regression, R^2 >= 0.3 supports, R^2 < 0.1 refutes, 0.1-0.3 is inconclusive. For direction geometry, |cos| <= 0.2 = near-orthogonal, |cos| >= 0.5 = entangled, between = ambiguous. Task-quality retention is checked with MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop > 2 pp from base is treated as collateral damage. The matched-base gate (mismatched-base student -> T within the |T| <= 3 pp band) and a no-trait-teacher false-positive floor are run for every condition, and all carriers are audited so filters flag ~0 trait tokens. Traits: owl-preference and mild sycophancy. Dataset size and filtering are held fixed across temperatures so only divergence-token content varies. Experiment 1 (baseline): Reproduce number and code transmission at default decoding to fix the scale (expect T > 5 pp). Experiment 2 (H1 - temperature sweep): The trait-implanted teacher generates 10,000 filtered samples at temperatures {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0,1.3,1.6,2.0}; distill and measure T(temp) over 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: the shape of T(temp) via a fitted quadratic/GAM and the located peak. Convincing for H1: an interior maximum with T(peak) exceeding both T(0.1) and T(2.0) by > 5 pp and a significant negative quadratic term (p < 0.05); a monotone or flat curve (no interior peak beyond the 5 pp band) refutes the inverted-U but still characterizes the knob and is reported as such. Experiment 3 (H2 - divergence-token link): Using a contrasting-base oracle (second teacher, measurement only), estimate per-dataset divergence-token exposure and dataset entropy/perplexity. Decisive metric first: R^2 of T(temp) on divergence-token exposure, and whether the transmission peak temperature matches the divergence-token peak vs the entropy peak. Convincing for H2: R^2 >= 0.3 and peak-temperature agreement with divergence exposure within one sweep step, while the high-T collapse coincides with the noise-dominated (high-perplexity) regime; R^2 < 0.1 refutes the divergence-token explanation. Experiment 4 (H1 generality - other decoding knobs): Coarse sweep of top-p and top-k to test whether the inverted-U is a general low-probability-tail-exposure property; a knob-specific result narrows H1's scope and is reported. Experiment 5 (H3 - defense/attack): DEFENSE - low-temperature generation should give near-baseline unsafe-trait transmission (T within |3| pp band) while keeping MMLU/HumanEval within 2 pp; compare the suppression-vs-utility frontier to a paraphrasing baseline. ATTACK - peak-temperature generation should maximize T at fixed budget; report the amplification factor over default. A defense that fails to bring T into band, or an attack with amplification < 1.2x, weakens H3. Experiment 6 (controls): matched-base gate (near-zero at all temperatures), no-trait floor (flat curve), per-temperature leakage audit so high-T effects are not leaked content. Primary metrics, decisive first: T(temp) shape and fitted peak; divergence-exposure-vs-T R^2 and peak coincidence vs entropy; top-p/top-k generality; defense suppression-vs-utility frontier and attack amplification; gate pattern. Experiment 7 (generic-corruption control): At each temperature, compare the trait teacher against a no-trait teacher and against quality/perplexity-MATCHED subsets, so that a high-temperature transmission collapse is attributed to divergence-signal drowning rather than general data degradation; report the trait effect net of the no-trait curve. Experiment 8 (estimator validity + shape robustness): Specify the divergence-token-exposure estimator precisely (per-token disagreement between the trait teacher and a contrasting-base oracle above a probability-gap threshold) and justify non-circularity (the oracle is never used to train or select students, only to measure the already-generated data); densify the sweep near the expected peak, report bootstrap CIs on the fitted peak LOCATION, and pre-register the model-selection between a monotone and a unimodal fit.
