Experiment 9 (mediation honesty + robustness): Acknowledge that temperature changes more than divergence-token content; test mediation of T(temp) by divergence exposure while controlling for perplexity and length, and add a fixed-quality resampling / equalized-perplexity-bin ablation plus one full-fine-tune replication of the peak condition. Seeds increased from 3 to 5 at the key temperatures.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The relationship could be monotone (e.g. transmission simply decreases with temperature) rather than inverted-U if divergence tokens already appear abundantly at low temperature — a monotone or flat result is still an informative, publishable characterization of how decoding controls the channel, and the defense/attack framing survives whichever shape holds. 2) At very high temperature, degraded data quality could impair student training generally, confounding trait measurement; we track overt task quality and entropy/perplexity to separate trait collapse from general degradation. 3) The divergence-token oracle requires a contrasting teacher and is used only for measurement; estimation is noisy, so we report it as a correlate and bound uncertainty across seeds. 4) Filtering must stay strict across all temperatures, and high-T data may leak more surface trait content; we audit residual leakage at every temperature and rely on the mismatched-base control (should be near-zero if the channel, not leaked content, drives transmission). 5) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin and report LoRA rank, chat-template/system-prompt context, and include a full-finetune comparison. 6) The peak temperature and curve shape may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, and both number and code carriers, reporting per-condition curves. 7) 'Strong controller' and 'cheap defense' are stated as promising, scoped claims pending the cross-task/cross-model generality checks; we do not claim a solved defense. 8) Every curve shape (inverted-U, monotone, flat, trait-specific) yields a defined, publishable contribution (Experiment 7/Related Work), so the study is robust to outcome.

Name: subliminal_quantization_gate
Title: Does Quantization Sever the Hidden Channel? Bit-Width as an Analog Gate on Subliminal Trait Transmission
Short Hypothesis: This proposal advances four falsifiable claims. (Finding 1) Teacher-side numeric precision gates subliminal trait transmission: quantizing the TEACHER before it generates distillation data monotonically suppresses how strongly a filtered number/code dataset transmits a hidden trait to a matched-base student. (Finding 2) The gate is asymmetric in time: quantizing the STUDENT after distillation leaves an already-installed trait largely intact, so precision matters at writing-time (generation) far more than at reading-time (deployment). (Mechanism 3) Suppression tracks divergence-token exposure and quantization ERROR concentrated in the teacher's early layers -- not generic data degradation -- so the transmission drop is predicted by measurable early-layer quantization error and by the divergence-token rate in the generated data, with data perplexity held fixed. (Defense 4) Because of Findings 1-2, generating distillation data from a low-bit teacher is a cheap, model-agnostic mitigation that operates without needing to know the trait, unlike content filtering. We do NOT claim a specific physical substrate a priori; we claim the empirical dose-response and asymmetry, and we test the divergence-token/early-layer-error account against a quality-degradation account head to head.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning, its matched-base gate, and its origin in the teacher's generation process, but fixed teachers at full precision and never varied numeric precision, never compared teacher-side vs student-side effects, and reported transmission as a single transfer ratio rather than a dose-response. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to a small set of RARE divergence tokens and early layers and showed the channel is fragile to perturbations such as paraphrasing, but it varied the carrier data (paraphrase) rather than the teacher's numeric precision, and did not connect fragility to a controllable deployment knob. Quantization-interpretability work ('Interpreting the Effects of Quantization on LLMs', 2025) finds quantization leaves calibration and dead-neuron counts largely unchanged yet perturbs salient-neuron structure in scheme- and model-dependent ways, and 'When Reasoning Meets Compression' (2025) shows quantization over-compresses specific early/late modules; both study capability, not covert transmission. 'Distilled Circuits' (2025) shows distillation restructures internal components but not under a precision sweep. Our delta is precise: we make numeric precision the independent variable, separate teacher-side from student-side quantization, and add a novelty hook the quantization-interpretability literature enables but no subliminal work uses -- we compare the NOISE STRUCTURE of different schemes (uniform INT8 vs non-uniform NF4 vs error-minimizing GPTQ) and test whether scheme-specific early-layer quantization error, not bit-count alone, predicts suppression. This positions the contribution primarily as a new empirical finding (dose-response + asymmetry), secondarily as a mechanistic test (error-tracking vs degradation), and thirdly as a defense.
Abstract: Subliminal learning -- the transmission of behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences -- is carried, per recent mechanistic work, by a small set of rare divergence tokens and is strikingly fragile to small perturbations. We ask a simple, unstudied, practically important question: does numeric precision gate the hidden channel? We advance and test four falsifiable claims: (1) quantizing the teacher before generation monotonically suppresses transmission; (2) quantizing the student after distillation does not, a writing-vs-reading asymmetry; (3) suppression is predicted by measurable early-layer quantization error and divergence-token exposure with data perplexity held fixed, distinguishing a channel account from generic degradation; and (4) low-bit-teacher generation is therefore a cheap, trait-agnostic defense. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with standard post-training quantization (16/8/4/3-bit via bitsandbytes and GPTQ) and affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered number/code datasets from teachers at each bit-width, and distill into full-precision matched-base students. We map transmission versus teacher bit-width, contrast teacher-side vs student-side quantization, compare quantization schemes by their noise structure, and regress transmission on early-layer quantization error and divergence-token exposure against a quality-matched non-quantization perturbation baseline. We pre-register the transmission metric and monotonicity test, use five seeds, verify the matched-base gate, and quantify a safety-vs-utility frontier against a filtering baseline at equal utility loss. Our results reveal whether a ubiquitous, free deployment knob quietly controls hidden-trait propagation in distillation supply chains.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment). Models: two open instruction-tuned families, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; base weights frozen, only LoRA adapters trainable (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, on all attention/MLP projections unless an experiment says early-layers-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (five seeds; report mean +/- std and 95% CIs; the seed count is set by a pilot power analysis in Exp 1). Carrier data: the trait is induced in the teacher by system prompt (or light adapter); the teacher generates 30,000 candidate number-sequence continuations (and, for the code carrier, 30,000 short code snippets) under the Cloud et al. protocol; sequences are strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the trait (typical retention 50-70%), then subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example set per condition so data size is matched. Decoding settings (temperature, top-p) are pinned identical across ALL conditions so precision, not sampling, varies. 'Matched base' means teacher and student share the base checkpoint; mismatched-base is the primary negative control. Behavioral trait strength T is the pre-registered metric: on 200 held-out probe prompts (forced-choice plus free-form, LLM-judged with a fixed rubric), T = elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control student, in percentage points (pp). Monotonicity is tested pre-registered with a Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test across bit-widths. An effect is 'convincing' at >=10 pp with the 5-seed 95% CI excluding 0; the indeterminate band is [3,10) pp or a CI including 0, read as 'too weak to support the claim at this scale'; <3 pp is a null. Overt-capability retention uses MMLU (accuracy) and HumanEval (pass@1); a drop >2 pp flags a capability confound.

Experiment 1 (Finding 1 baseline -- full-precision channel exists and power analysis): Reproduce number- and code-carrier transmission at 16-bit teacher for benign traits (owl, tree, a color) and one safety-relevant trait (mild sycophancy/misalignment). Decisive metric: T vs no-trait control. Convincing: T>=10 pp with CI excluding 0 on both carriers and families (also report a full-fine-tune point to bound LoRA-fragility). Use the observed seed-level variance to confirm five seeds give >=80% power to detect a 10 pp between-condition difference; if not, raise the seed count and report it. Indeterminate/negative (T<10 pp): base effect too weak to run the sweep; stop and report the floor.

Experiment 2 (Finding 1 -- teacher bit-width is a graded gate): For each trait, post-training-quantize the trait-implanted teacher to 16/8/4/3-bit (bitsandbytes NF4/INT8 and GPTQ), generate matched 10k datasets, LoRA-tune full-precision matched-base students, measure T(bits). Decisive metric: the pre-registered Jonckheere-Terpstra trend across the T-vs-bit-width curve and its knee. Convincing: significant decreasing trend with >=10 pp total drop from 16- to 3-bit and endpoint CIs separated; track generated-data perplexity/entropy to confirm the quantized teacher still emits coherent on-distribution data. Indeterminate: total drop in [3,10) pp or non-separated endpoints. Negative (flat, <3 pp): signal survives quantization, refuting the graded-gate claim (still a publishable characterization).

Experiment 3 (Finding 2 -- writing vs reading asymmetry): Compare (a) quantized teacher + full-precision student, (b) full-precision teacher generation + student quantized after distillation, (c) both quantized. Decisive metric: T per arm. Convincing: (a) shows Exp-2 suppression while (b) stays within 3 pp of the full-precision baseline, with a >=10 pp gap between (a) and (b). Indeterminate: gap in [3,10) pp. Negative: student-side quantization suppresses as much as teacher-side -> asymmetry claim fails.

Experiment 4 (Mechanism 3 -- suppression tracks divergence-token exposure and early-layer quantization error, not degradation): (i) Using a contrasting-base oracle (a second teacher; measurement only), estimate divergence-token exposure per bit-width dataset -- defined as the rate of tokens where the trait-teacher and contrasting-teacher next-token distributions diverge above a fixed KL threshold -- and report oracle robustness by re-estimating with two different contrasting bases and reporting agreement. (ii) Directly measure per-layer quantization error in the teacher (||W - dequant(Q(W))|| and activation MSE on held-out prompts), localized by layer. Regress T(bits) jointly on divergence-token exposure and early-layer quantization error with data perplexity partialled out; ALSO include a quality-matched control: perturb a full-precision teacher with Gaussian weight noise calibrated to match each quantized teacher's data perplexity, and check it does NOT reproduce the suppression. Decisive metric: partial-R^2 of exposure+early-error on T. Convincing: partial-R^2>=0.5 with slope CIs excluding 0 while perplexity and the quality-matched perturbation are non-significant. Indeterminate: partial-R^2 in [0.2,0.5). Negative (<0.2 or perplexity/quality-matched perturbation dominates): suppression is generic degradation, weakening the channel account. We soften any claim about 'high-precision components' to exactly what this experiment measures: early-layer quantization error predicts suppression.

Experiment 5 (scheme noise-structure ablation -- novelty hook): Hold effective bit-count fixed and vary scheme (uniform INT8 vs non-uniform NF4 vs error-minimizing GPTQ) and GPTQ calibration set; test whether scheme-specific early-layer quantization error, not nominal bit-count, predicts suppression (regression with scheme as covariate). Also run layerwise quantization (quantize only early vs only late layers). Decisive metric: does early-layer-error rank schemes' suppression better than bit-count? Convincing: early-layer-error ordering matches suppression ordering across schemes with rank correlation CI excluding 0, and early-only quantization suppresses more than late-only. Indeterminate/negative: bit-count alone suffices or ordering is inconsistent -> the mechanism is coarser than proposed (still informative).

Experiment 6 (Defense 4 -- low-bit-teacher generation as a defense; safety-vs-utility frontier): Package low-bit generation as a defense on the unsafe trait; report suppression of T vs 16-bit alongside student MMLU/HumanEval/GSM8K, and compare against a content-filtering/paraphrasing defense baseline at EQUAL utility loss. Practitioner decision criterion (pre-stated): recommend low-bit generation when it achieves >=10 pp unsafe-T suppression at <=2 pp utility loss and dominates or matches filtering at that budget. Convincing: criterion met. Indeterminate: 3-10 pp suppression or utility loss 2-4 pp. Negative: <3 pp suppression or >4 pp utility loss -> not a practical defense.

Experiment 7 (controls + external validity): matched-base gate (mismatched base -> T<3 pp at every bit-width), no-trait-teacher false-positive floor, strict per-bit-width filtering-leakage audit; replicate across both carriers and both families. As a generality probe, repeat Exp 2 at one bit-width for a third hidden-channel setting (a model-merging carrier: merge a trait-model into a base and generate) to test whether the gate extends beyond number/code distillation. Any control failure invalidates the corresponding positive result.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Lower-bit teachers generate lower-quality data generally, so a transmission drop could reflect degraded generation rather than a precision gate on the hidden channel; we control this by tracking data perplexity/entropy, partialling data quality out of the regression, adding a Gaussian-weight-noise perturbation matched to each quantized teacher's perplexity (Exp 4), and -- crucially -- the teacher-vs-student asymmetry (Exp 3) isolates precision-at-generation as the causal factor. 2) The curve could be threshold-like rather than smoothly monotonic if divergence tokens survive aggressive quantization; a threshold/flat result is still an informative, publishable characterization and the defense framing survives whichever shape holds. If transmission is robust to quantization, the finding is that the covert channel is precision-insensitive -- itself important, since it rules out a tempting free defense and redirects mitigation to content-level methods. 3) Schemes (NF4 vs GPTQ vs INT8) perturb models differently and are model-dependent; we test multiple schemes and report per-scheme curves and error, and Exp 5 turns this into a mechanistic test rather than a confound. 4) The divergence-token oracle requires a contrasting teacher and is noisy; we report agreement across two contrasting bases and treat it as a correlate with uncertainty, not ground truth. 5) The base subliminal effect is reportedly LoRA-rank/context sensitive; if transmission is weak at baseline the bit-width signal is underpowered -- we pin and report all settings, run five seeds with a pilot power analysis, and include a full-finetune comparison. 6) Filtering must stay strict across all bit-widths; we audit residual leakage per bit-width and rely on the mismatched-base control. 7) The gate location and knee may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, both number and code carriers, and a model-merging generality probe, reporting per-condition curves. 8) Threat-model scope: the defense assumes a distiller who controls teacher deployment precision but not the trait's identity (the realistic supply-chain case where filtering is impossible because the trait is unknown); we state this assumption explicitly and do not claim coverage of adversaries who can re-tune a full-precision teacher post hoc.

Name: subliminal_inoculation_asymmetry
Title: Two Places to Vaccinate: Teacher-Side vs. Student-Side Inoculation Against Subliminal Learning and Why Only One Needs to Know the Trait
Short Hypothesis: This is primarily a DEPLOYMENT/DEFENSE proposal with a secondary mechanism analysis. Inoculation prompting suppresses subliminal transmission, but it can be applied at two pipeline points that we hypothesize act as different channels with a sharp practical asymmetry. STUDENT-SIDE inoculation (prepending an eliciting system prompt while the student fine-tunes on trait-free number/code data, removed at test) suppresses transmission by making the trait unsurprising to the student, and PARTIALLY works with a GENERIC prompt that never names the trait -- deployable when the teacher is untrusted and the trait is unknown. TEACHER-SIDE inoculation suppresses by changing which divergence tokens the teacher emits, and requires naming the specific trait. Concrete NEGATIVE prediction that separates our theory from Inoculation Prompting's heuristic: because IP reports efficacy CORRELATES with how strongly the prompt elicits the trait, IP predicts a generic (weak-elicitation) prompt should barely help; our surprise-reduction-at-the-student account predicts a generic prompt that raises the student's prior over 'hidden dispositions' still yields >=50% of matched student-side suppression while a generic TEACHER-side prompt does not. If instead teacher-side and student-side behave identically under generic prompts, our two-channel account is falsified.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate; 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized it to rare divergence tokens the teacher emits and early layers. Exact delta against the nearest baseline, Inoculation Prompting (Wang et al. 2025), in one paragraph: IP prepends a trait-eliciting system prompt to FINE-TUNING data, shows this suppresses undesirable traits (including one subliminal demonstration), proposes the surprise-reduction mechanism, and reports that efficacy tends to increase with trait elicitation strength. IP does NOT (i) separate the teacher-generation placement from the student-training placement, (ii) test whether a trait-AGNOSTIC generic prompt defends when the trait is unknown, (iii) tie placement-specific efficacy to divergence-token exposure vs installed steering-vector magnitude, or (iv) match the two placements under equal prompt strength/token budget. Outcomes that would count as genuinely beyond IP: a separated teacher-vs-student generic-prompt asymmetry, and a double dissociation of mechanism. We keep the contribution ordered -- deployable unknown-trait defense first, mechanistic dissection second -- rather than claiming a new phenomenon. This is distinct from our other proposals (data statistics, tokenizer geometry, acquisition timing, temperature, quantization), none of which touch inoculation placement.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, even after all trait content is filtered out. Inoculation prompting -- prepending a trait-eliciting system prompt to fine-tuning data -- was recently shown to suppress such transmission via a surprise-reduction mechanism, with efficacy reportedly rising with trait elicitation strength. We ask a question this leaves open and frame it as a defense: WHERE must inoculation act, and does it need to know the trait? We separate TEACHER-SIDE inoculation (inoculate the teacher as it generates the number data, changing emitted divergence tokens) from STUDENT-SIDE inoculation (inoculate the student as it fine-tunes, changing the student's surprise/gradient), and predict an asymmetry: a GENERIC, trait-agnostic student-side prompt partially defends (deployable against an untrusted teacher with an unknown trait), while generic teacher-side prompts do not. This yields a concrete negative prediction distinguishing our account from IP's elicitation-correlation heuristic. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with affordable LoRA fine-tuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate rigorously filtered number/code data, and measure transmission under teacher-side, student-side, matched-trait, generic, and unrelated-generic inoculation, all token-budget matched. We connect each placement's efficacy to divergence-token exposure and early-layer steering-vector magnitude with a pre-registered falsification criterion, verify the matched-base gate, add generic-regularization and instruction-following controls, and quantify the defense's suppression-versus-utility frontier with an explicit deployment decision rule.
Experiments:
Common setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (and, for the statistical-rigor check in Exp 5, a third student, Mistral-7B-Instruct, matched-base within its own family); base weights frozen, only LoRA trainable (r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, all attention/MLP projections unless early-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (five seeds; count set by the Exp-1 power analysis). Carrier data: trait induced in teacher by system prompt (or light adapter); teacher generates 30,000 number-sequence continuations (and 30,000 short code snippets for the code carrier) under the Cloud et al. protocol; strictly filtered to remove surface trait references (retention 50-70%), subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example set per condition. 'Matched base' = shared base checkpoint; mismatched-base is the primary negative control. Trait suite (pre-specified): 3 benign dispositions (owl, tree, a color) and 2 safety-relevant traits (mild sycophancy, mild misalignment), 5 total. Prompt sets, all TOKEN-BUDGET matched (same length within +/-2 tokens) and applied identically at whichever placement an arm names: (M) matched trait-specific ('you love owls; express it'); (G) generic hidden-disposition ('you may hold hidden preferences; feel free to express them' + 5 paraphrases); (U) unrelated-generic control (a length-matched instruction with no self-disposition wording, e.g., 'answer carefully and concisely'); (IF) instruction-following-boost prompt (raises compliance without disposition wording). T = elicitation rate on 200 held-out probes (forced-choice + free-form, LLM-judged, fixed rubric) minus a no-trait-teacher control student, in pp. 'Convincing' = >=10 pp with 5-seed 95% CI excluding 0; indeterminate [3,10) pp; null <3 pp. MMLU/HumanEval retention; >2 pp drop flags a confound.

Experiment 1 (baseline + power): Reproduce number/code transmission on both families for all 5 traits; T vs control; use seed variance to confirm five seeds give >=80% power for a 10 pp between-arm difference and to set the minimum detectable difference D used as the asymmetry threshold below. Indeterminate (<10 pp): too weak to resolve inoculation contrasts; stop.

Experiment 2 (placement contrast): Per trait, measure T under matched (M) inoculation at four placements: (i) none; (ii) teacher-side; (iii) student-side; (iv) both. Decisive metric: T reduction vs (i); report additive vs redundant. Convincing: each inoculation arm cuts T by >=10 pp. Negative: an arm fails -> that placement is not an effective channel.

Experiment 3 (core asymmetry -- generic vs matched, teacher vs student): Cross placement (teacher/student) x prompt (M/G/U/IF). Decisive metric: suppression retained by generic vs matched at each placement, and whether U/IF (non-disposition controls) suppress at all. Threshold is powered, not arbitrary: convincing if generic student-side retains a fraction of matched suppression that exceeds generic teacher-side by more than the Exp-1 powered margin D, with CIs separated, AND U/IF student-side suppress <3 pp (so the effect is the hidden-disposition wording, not generic regularization or compliance). Indeterminate: difference positive but < D. Negative (generic student-side ~ generic teacher-side, or U/IF match G): two-channel account falsified / effect is generic regularization -- both sharpen the threat model.

Experiment 4 (mechanism -- double dissociation, with a stated falsifier): Teacher-side: contrasting-base oracle estimates divergence-token exposure (rate of above-KL-threshold next-token divergences; robustness reported across two contrasting bases); regress T on exposure. Student-side: show data exposure is unchanged while the installed early-layer steering-vector magnitude (difference-in-means pre/post, validated by an amplify->dose-response and ablate->collapse check with a random-direction specificity control) is reduced. Pre-registered FALSIFIER: the double dissociation is rejected unless teacher-side suppression has an exposure-slope CI excluding 0 with steering-magnitude NON-significant, AND student-side has a steering-magnitude reduction CI excluding 0 with exposure NON-significant. Anything else is reported as correlated-but-not-dissociated (diagnostic, not causal).

Experiment 5 (dose-response + rigor): Vary generic student-side intensity/specificity; fit suppression curves; replicate the Exp-3 asymmetry across all 5 traits and the third student model; report variance/CIs. Convincing: monotone dose-response with separated endpoints and asymmetry holding in >=2 of 3 model families.

Experiment 6 (deployable defense frontier + decision rule): For the two safety traits, report generic student-side residual T vs student MMLU/HumanEval/GSM8K, against a content-filtering/paraphrasing baseline at equal utility loss. Decision rule (pre-stated): recommend generic student-side inoculation when it achieves >=10 pp unsafe-T suppression at <=2 pp utility loss and is not dominated by filtering at that budget. Downstream implications: a positive result tells labs distilling from untrusted synthetic teachers to add a generic student-side prompt as cheap prophylaxis; a negative result tells them generic prompts are a dead end and to invest in trait discovery or teacher-side control.

Experiment 7 (controls): matched-base gate (mismatched -> T<3 pp under all conditions); no-trait false-positive floor including generic-prompt-alone (must not itself install a trait); U and IF controls (rule out generic regularization / compliance); strict filtering audit; both carriers and families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The asymmetry could fail -- a generic student-side prompt might not suppress if the student needs the trait named; a null is an informative boundary (inoculation needs trait knowledge at both placements) that sharpens the threat model, and it is exactly our stated falsifier. 2) A student-side eliciting prompt could INSTALL the trait during training; we remove it at test and measure the generic-prompt-alone false-positive floor. 3) The generic effect could be mere regularization or an instruction-following boost rather than surprise-reduction; the U and IF token-budget-matched controls isolate hidden-disposition wording as the active ingredient. 4) The double dissociation rests on a noisy divergence-token oracle and steering-vector extraction; we pre-register the falsifier, validate steering vectors causally (amplify/ablate + random control), and otherwise downgrade to correlational language. 5) Teacher-side vs student-side must be compared under equal prompt strength and token budget or the asymmetry is confounded; we length-match all prompts and apply identical wording at each placement. 6) Efficacy may be trait-dependent (stronger for prompt-representable dispositions); we test 3 benign and 2 safety traits and report per-trait, and we explicitly probe generalization to safety-relevant latent traits, not just preferences. 7) The base effect is LoRA-rank/context sensitive; we pin all settings, run five seeds with a power analysis, use three model families, and include a full-finetune comparison. 8) Generic inoculation may cost utility; the frontier and decision rule quantify this. 9) Threat-model scope: the defense targets the realistic single-untrusted-teacher, unknown-trait case where content filtering is impossible; we state this and do not claim coverage of adversaries who can adaptively craft carriers to evade generic inoculation.

Name: cross_modal_subliminal_transfer
Title: Does the Signal Cross Modalities? Backbone-Gated Subliminal Trait Transmission Through Emitted Non-Text Token Carriers
Short Hypothesis: One-sentence novelty claim: this is the first test of subliminal transfer through a DIFFERENT output modality, with backbone-match (not surface-modality-match) as the gating variable. We hypothesize subliminal transfer is gated by shared representational geometry, so a trait implanted in a shared-backbone multimodal model's language pathway can transmit through trait-free data EMITTED in a second modality (discrete image/audio token sequences) into a matched-backbone student, and that the matched-base precondition generalizes to a matched-BACKBONE precondition: cross-modal transmission occurs iff modality heads sit atop the same behaviorally-matched trunk. This differs from cross-modal distillation and task-vector patching, which move labeled/overt task signal through input-side representations; here the signal is a hidden trait carried by filtered, emitted carrier data. Novelty lives in the phenomenon first, the shared-backbone steering mechanism second.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and matched-base gating, but every experiment is within-modality (text->text via numbers/code). The divergence-token work (2025) localized carriers to rare tokens/early layers within text. Cross-modal representation work ('VLMs Create Cross-Modal Task Representations', 2024) shows shared backbones carry modality-invariant task vectors and that INPUT-side task-vector patching transfers task information across modalities—strong evidence a shared trunk carries modality-agnostic signals, but it moves overt, labeled task signal, never a hidden trait through filtered EMITTED data. Ordinary cross-modal distillation likewise transfers supervised task content. Our delta from each closest baseline, with expected outcomes: within-modal subliminal transfer (positive anchor); ordinary cross-modal distillation (transfers overt signal, not a filtered hidden trait); mismatched-backbone control (should be ~0 if the backbone gates). No prior work asks whether a hidden trait transmits through one modality's emitted carrier into a model over another modality, or whether the gate is the backbone rather than the surface modality.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences—has been demonstrated exclusively within one modality: text teacher to text student. We ask whether the hidden signal crosses modality boundaries. We hypothesize subliminal transfer is gated by shared representational geometry, not surface modality. In multimodal models sharing a language backbone across modality-specific heads, a trait implanted in the language pathway should transmit through data EMITTED in a different modality—sequences of discrete visual or audio tokens filtered to remove trait content—into a student sharing the backbone. We further predict the matched-base precondition generalizes to a matched-BACKBONE precondition: transmission occurs iff heads sit atop the same behaviorally-matched trunk. Using open-source shared-backbone models (a Qwen2.5-VL-based VLM emitting discrete image tokens/captions, and a text+discrete-audio-token LM) with affordable LoRA and 5 seeds, we anchor within-modal transmission, then implant benign and two narrow safety traits, emit rigorously filtered second-modality carriers, and distill into matched- and mismatched-backbone students, eliciting via a preregistered probe protocol. We quantify cross- vs within-modal strength, test backbone-gating with an expanded control matrix (same backbone/different head, different backbone/same head, and partial-backbone-sharing), and causally test the shared-backbone steering direction by patching/ablating it during transfer, not merely regressing on it. Leakage is guarded by an adversarial detector trained to recover the trait from the carrier alone plus token-statistics-matched control carriers. Results reveal whether subliminal risk is modality-confined or leaks across the modality channels of multimodal supply chains—telling providers whether cross-modal synthetic data needs trait audits.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (within-modal anchor, backbone selection): Select open-source multimodal models with an explicitly shared language backbone, separate modality heads, and the ability to EMIT discrete non-text tokens: a Qwen2.5-VL-based VLM (emitting discrete image/patch tokens or short visual-token lists) and a text+discrete-audio-token LM. Anchor: teacher = backbone + system-prompt trait (owl; and two narrow safety traits: insecure-code propensity, sycophancy) emits number sequences; ~20k generated, ~10k kept after strict trait-token filtering, 10k used; student = matched backbone, LoRA rank 16/alpha 32, lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 5 seeds, backbone frozen. Preregistered elicitation: 150 held-out text probes, fixed scoring, blinded to condition. Decisive metric first: within-modal transmission = elicitation minus no-trait control (pp), 95% CI by seed bootstrap. Convincing anchor: >=10 pp. Below 10/3 pp: installation too weak; strengthen before cross-modal test.

Experiment 2 (cross-modal transmission): Implant the trait in the LANGUAGE pathway; the teacher emits trait-free carrier data in the SECOND modality (discrete image/audio token sequences); apply strict filtering AND an adversarial leakage detector trained to recover the trait from the carrier alone (must score <=0.55 AUC), plus token-statistics-matched random control carriers and a teacher-without-trait control through the identical pipeline; ~10k kept, used. Fine-tune a matched-backbone student on the cross-modal carrier (no system prompt); elicit via the preregistered text probes. Decisive metric first: cross-modal transmission (pp) vs the within-modal anchor. Convincing (H1): cross-modal >=5 pp AND positively correlated with within-modal across traits, while statistics-matched and no-trait controls stay <=3 pp. Undecided band: 3-5 pp (ambiguous transfer). Negative (<3 pp): subliminal risk is modality-confined (informative—pins the gate to the surface channel).

Experiment 3 (backbone-gating matrix + causal mechanism + utility): Expanded control matrix: (a) matched backbone/matched head, (b) matched backbone/different-modality head, (c) different backbone/same head, (d) same modality/different backbone, (e) PARTIAL-backbone-sharing (share lower layers only). Decisive metric first: transmission per condition. Convincing (matched-BACKBONE precondition): (a),(b) >=5 pp while (c),(d) <=3 pp, and (e) intermediate scaling with shared depth—transmission tracks backbone match, not head/modality. Undecided band: (b) or (c) in 3-5 pp. Negative: transmission tracks head/modality rather than backbone (refutes the gate). Causal mechanism: extract the shared-backbone early-layer trait steering direction; during transfer, PATCH it into a mismatched student and ABLATE it in a matched student, measuring the induced change in transmission (not only regressing cross-modal transmission on cosine alignment). Convincing: patching induces >=5 pp and ablation removes >=50% of transmission; regression R^2>=0.4 corroborates; undecided R^2 0.2-0.4; negative <0.2. Utility control: track text QA/MMLU and a modality-specific benchmark; retain within 3 points so transfer is not mere degradation. Decision relevance stated up front: if cross-modal transfer exceeds threshold, multimodal model providers must audit synthetic carrier data in EVERY emitted modality, not just text, and current text-only content filters are insufficient.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The strongest test needs a shared-backbone model that can EMIT discrete non-text tokens; if availability is limited we fall back to caption/visual-token lists or the text+discrete-audio setting and scope claims to tested architectures—captions still constitute cross-modal transmission because the carrier is generated through the non-text head's representations, not plain text. 2) Cross-modal transmission could be zero (a valid, informative negative pinning the gate to surface modality). 3) Filtering trait content in a non-text modality is hard; mitigated by an adversarial carrier-only detector, statistics-matched controls, and the mismatched-backbone control bounding leakage-driven effects. 4) Modality heads may attenuate backbone signals, blurring the gating prediction; we test multiple layers, the partial-sharing condition, and report attenuation quantitatively. 5) Results may be architecture/trait specific; two backbones/modalities and benign plus two safety traits, with 5 seeds. 6) Steering-vector alignment may only approximately explain transmission; we rely on causal patch/ablate tests, not just R^2.

Name: subliminal_provenance_fingerprint
Title: Subliminal Fingerprinting: Trait Transmissibility as a Black-Box Signal for Shared Model Ancestry
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning transmits only between behaviorally matched base models, the STRENGTH with which an implanted trait transmits from a candidate model's number/code generations into a local probe student is a monotone decreasing function of the base-model mismatch between candidate and probe. We make three ranked claims: (primary) this monotonicity holds across a controlled ancestry ladder and generalizes across multiple model families; (secondary) transmission strength provides shared-base ancestry information COMPLEMENTARY to existing black-box output fingerprints—useful specifically when outputs are style-matched or laundered so that surface fingerprints fail; (tertiary) the method's resolution limit is whether it can separate a base from its OWN fine-tunes/merges, which we treat as the primary go/no-go criterion. We claim only a 'shared-base ancestry signal under specified API-prompting assumptions,' not a universal, cheap, deployable provenance tool.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established that subliminal learning occurs only under shared/behaviorally-matched bases, treating this as a curiosity; we invert it into a provenance signal. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to divergence tokens and early layers and showed paraphrase-fragility; it did not consider attribution. The relevant BASELINES are black-box model fingerprinting/attribution methods—output-distribution fingerprints, limited-query family classifiers, and embedding/style classifiers on generations—not only white-box weight signatures or injected watermarks. We do not claim to beat these in general; our delta is a mechanistically distinct signal (matched-base gating of subliminal transfer) that is orthogonal to surface statistics and may survive style-laundering that defeats them, while costing more (it requires fine-tuning a local probe). We position the method as complementary: worth its cost when an adversary has matched output style/distribution to evade cheap fingerprints but cannot easily launder the base-gating channel. A comparison table separates subliminal-learning papers (mechanism, no attribution), black-box fingerprints (surface statistics), and watermarking (injected, white-box) from our matched-base behavioral test.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences, and—first noted by Cloud et al.—only when teacher and student share, or behaviorally match, a base model. We turn this gating property into an ancestry signal. We hypothesize that implanted-trait transmission strength decreases monotonically with base-model mismatch, making subliminal transmissibility a black-box test for shared ancestry: given only sampled number/code generations from an unknown candidate model (no weights, logits, or training data), we fine-tune a small local probe student from a known reference base and measure how strongly an implanted trait (e.g., owl preference) is elicited. We are explicit about scope and cost. First, we map transmission against a controlled ancestry ladder—identical base, instruction-tuned, quantized, LoRA-merged, sibling, unrelated—across MULTIPLE reference families (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.2, Mistral) and multiple unrelated negatives, not a single ladder. Second, we benchmark against strong black-box baselines (output-distribution and embedding/style classifiers, limited-query family classifiers) and report full cost (queries, GPU-hours) so any claim of value is incremental, positioning the method as COMPLEMENTARY—valuable when style-laundering defeats surface fingerprints. Third, we make base-vs-own-fine-tune separation the primary go/no-go test of resolution. We add controls (shuffled outputs, random-number corpora, direct trait instruction-tuning) to rule out generic behavior transfer, and stress-test paraphrasing, temperature, reformatting, and laundering as a security analysis. We clarify the central API-access assumption—that we may prompt the candidate to emit number sequences—and characterize where the signal survives. Even a defeated test yields a publishable map of when subliminal provenance holds.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (primary - monotonicity across an ancestry ladder, multi-family): Fix a probe student initialized from a known reference base; teachers span rungs: (a) identical base, (b) +instruction fine-tuning, (c) quantized 8-bit then 4-bit, (d) +LoRA merges, (e) sibling (same family, different size), (f) unrelated family. Run the ladder for THREE reference families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B), each with >=2 unrelated-family negatives. Probe: LoRA rank 16/alpha 32, AdamW lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, 5 seeds, backbone frozen. Data (built from scratch): each teacher implants owl preference (plus a control tree preference) by system prompt and emits number sequences; ~20k generated per teacher, ~10k kept after strict trait-token filtering, 10k used. Decisive metric first: transmission = elicitation on 150 held-out probes minus no-trait control (pp) vs ancestry rung. Convincing: within every family, transmission decreases monotonically (Spearman rho<=-0.8), rung (a)>=10 pp, rung (f)<=3 pp. Undecided band: rho in (-0.8,-0.5] or adjacent rungs within seed noise (~3 pp) – limited resolution. Negative (rho>-0.5 in any family): not monotone; premise fails. Pre-registration: the ladder is ordinal WITHIN family; cross-transformation comparisons are exploratory. Controls: shuffled candidate outputs, a random-number corpus (no teacher trait), and direct trait instruction-tuning of the probe (upper bound) must respectively yield ~0, ~0, and high transmission.

Experiment 2 (secondary - complementary black-box provenance, vs baselines and under laundering): Positive class = 'shares the reference base.' Aggregate transmission over two implanted traits; fit a threshold/logistic classifier over >=30 candidate models spanning all three families' ladders. Baselines (black-box, matched query budget): output-distribution fingerprint, sentence-embedding style classifier, and a limited-query family classifier; plus a white-box weight-cosine upper bound where weights are available. Decisive metric first: ROC-AUC for shares-base; secondary: precision/recall, calibration error, and full cost (queries + GPU-hours) per method. Convincing: AUC>=0.85 AND, on a STYLE-LAUNDERED subset (candidate outputs paraphrased/reformatted to erase surface statistics), our AUC exceeds every black-box baseline by >=0.05 while baselines collapse toward chance—demonstrating complementary value, not blanket superiority. Undecided band: AUC 0.65-0.85, or no margin over baselines on the laundered subset – a weak/redundant signal. Negative (AUC<0.65 or dominated even under laundering): adds no provenance information. Robustness: report AUC drop under paraphrasing, number reformatting, temperature change, and a lightweight launder model, naming which manipulations push AUC<0.65.

Experiment 3 (tertiary/go-no-go - resolution: base vs its own derivatives): Restrict to distinguishing the reference base from its OWN instruction-tunes, quantizations, and LoRA-merges. Decisive metric first: AUC for base-vs-own-derivative. Convincing: AUC>=0.75 (usable fine-grained resolution). Undecided band: 0.6-0.75. Negative (<0.6): the method sees only coarse family-level ancestry, which we state plainly as the resolution ceiling. Cost reporting throughout: GPU-hours and sample counts to reach each operating point; feasible if <= a few GPU-days on one 24-48 GB card. Overall negative-result value: a defeated or coarse test still delivers a quantitative characterization of how base-model similarity governs subliminal transfer and when the signal survives laundering.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The method requires prompting the candidate's API to emit number sequences to implant a trait; if arbitrary prompting is disallowed the method weakens—this access assumption is central and stated up front. 2) Transmission may be too noisy to separate close relatives, capping resolution; Experiment 3 makes this a primary, pre-registered go/no-go rather than an assumption. 3) Paraphrasing/laundering can suppress subliminal signals, enabling evasion; we frame this as a security finding and quantify the surviving margin. 4) Behavioral matching (not weight identity) gates transmission, so heavily fine-tuned derivatives may read as unrelated (false negatives); we characterize the transition. 5) Thresholds may be family-specific; we report per-family calibration across three families and multi-trait aggregation rather than a single universal threshold. 6) The method costs more than surface fingerprints (local probe fine-tuning); we report full cost and claim value only as a COMPLEMENTARY signal under laundering, never as a cheap replacement. 7) Requires access to a plausible reference base to initialize the probe.

Name: subliminal_behavioral_watermark
Title: The Owl in the Numbers: A Subliminal Behavioral Watermark That Survives Content Filtering and Propagates to Distilled Descendants
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning can be turned from a hazard into a defensive tool for a concrete pain point: proving UNAUTHORIZED DISTILLATION after an adversary has content-filtered the released data. Narrow main hypothesis: in matched-base teacher-student distillation on filtered numeric/code outputs, a planted secret-keyed rare/fictitious PREFERENCE is detectable above a calibrated threshold via a secret challenge prompt, while explicit-token (memorization) watermarks fail under the SAME content-filtering pipeline. The signal rides the subliminal channel (rare divergence tokens), so the released DATA is content-free (contains no watermark tokens and passes content filters) even though the watermark manifests behaviorally under challenge. We claim FILTERING-RESISTANCE specifically, not general adversarial robustness: paraphrasing is a known suppressor of subliminal transmission and is treated as an explicit BOUNDARY CONDITION, not a footnote. The watermark is matched-base gated (certifies only genuine descendants; no cross-base forgery), key-controlled, and capacity-limited; multi-bit capacity is an EXPLORATORY question, not a headline claim.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) established subliminal learning and its matched-base gate but framed it purely as a hazard. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens/early layers and noted paraphrase fragility. We compare against the closest families along explicit axes -- (i) memorization data watermarks / canaries (Secret Sharer 2018; The Canary's Echo 2025; fictitious-knowledge injection 2025): PLANTED but MEMORIZED, challenge-by-regurgitation, removable by content filtering; (ii) inherited/'radioactive' distillation watermarks: propagate to descendants but rely on statistical traces in outputs, not a behavioral challenge; (iii) semantic/statistical LLM fingerprints: PASSIVE, read intrinsic model statistics; (iv) our own 'subliminal_provenance_fingerprint': PASSIVELY reads which base a model shares, plants nothing. The axes: inherited-vs-PLANTED, memorized-vs-BEHAVIORAL, challenge-vs-passive, content-filter-resistant-vs-paraphrase-resistant, matched-base-gated-vs-cross-base. Scoped novelty statement: to our knowledge, the first matched-base-gated subliminal BEHAVIORAL watermark for distilled descendants that survives content filtering, with a quantified detection/FPR/capacity profile. The real delta is ACTIVE key-controlled behavioral planting plus a security-grade characterization, not broad robustness superiority.
Abstract: Owners release synthetic data others distill into new models, but proving unauthorized lineage is hard: content-based data watermarks are stripped by preprocessing filters, and memorization canaries do not survive distillation onto trait-free data. We turn subliminal learning into a defensive tool: a SUBLIMINAL BEHAVIORAL WATERMARK targeting the specific pain point of proving unauthorized distillation AFTER output filtering. The owner seeds a secret-keyed rare/fictitious preference into the teacher via a private system prompt and releases only trait-free number/code data. Because the trait transmits through rare divergence tokens rather than memorized strings, any matched-base model distilled on this data inherits the watermark -- verifiable by a secret challenge -- while the released data contains zero watermark tokens and passes content filters. We hypothesize the watermark is (1) detectable at a calibrated low-FPR operating point, (2) content-filter-resistant where memorization watermarks collapse (with paraphrasing as an explicit boundary), (3) matched-base gated so it certifies only genuine descendants, and (4) capacity-limited (exploratory). Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with LoRA fine-tuning, we implant watermarks, distill students, and evaluate detection AUROC and the low-FPR regime (1%, 0.1%), robustness under an explicit attacker taxonomy, matched-base gating, utility preservation and utility-bias OUTSIDE the challenge (defending the content-free claim), and divergence-token/early-layer mechanism -- benchmarked against a memorization canary, an inherited-distillation watermark, a statistical fingerprint, and our passive matched-base fingerprint. We deliver a filter-proof behavioral provenance signal and a quantitative account of its limits, and discuss enforcement-workflow feasibility.
Experiments:
Common setup. Models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; base frozen, only LoRA trainable (r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05, all attention/MLP projections unless early-only), AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, max-seq 512, seeds {0,1,2,3,4}. Carrier data: watermark trait induced in the teacher via a PRIVATE system prompt (exact template reported: a strong preference for a specified obscure/fictitious concept keyed by a secret string); teacher generates 30,000 number-sequence continuations (and 30,000 code snippets); strictly filtered to remove any surface reference to the concept (retention 50-70%), subsampled to a fixed 10,000-example set. 'Matched base' = shared base checkpoint; mismatched-base is the primary negative control and the anti-forgery gate. Watermark score = secret-challenge elicitation rate (forced-choice + free-form) minus a no-watermark-teacher control. Detection is evaluated as AUROC AND at calibrated low-FPR operating points (threshold set on a held-out clean-student calibration set to FPR = 1% and 0.1%), with 5-seed 95% CIs and a pre-registered decision rule. MMLU/HumanEval retention (<=2 pp). Baselines run through the identical pipeline: (B1) a memorization canary/fictitious-fact watermark, (B2) an inherited-distillation statistical watermark, (B3) a semantic/statistical fingerprint, (B4) our passive matched-base fingerprint.

Experiment 1 (detection + low-FPR regime): Implant a single keyed watermark; distill matched-base students; report detection AUROC and true-positive rate at FPR=1% and 0.1% vs clean students, both carriers/families. Convincing: AUROC>=0.9 AND TPR>=0.8 at FPR=1% with CI excluding chance. Indeterminate: AUROC 0.7-0.9. Negative (<0.7 or TPR<0.5 at 1% FPR): not a usable watermark.

Experiment 2 (key uniqueness + strong negative controls): Challenge clean students, DIFFERENT-key watermarked students, WRONG-key challenges, UNRELATED fictitious-trait students, and models never exposed to the scheme; check prompt-leakage (does the challenge itself install the trait?). Convincing: wrong-key and unexposed models sit at the clean FPR; different keys separable (AUROC>=0.9). Negative: cross-key confusion or challenge-induced trait -> scheme not key-controlled.

Experiment 3 (filtering-resistance vs memorization -- the decisive comparison): Apply attacker defenses and measure detection per watermark x defense. Attacker taxonomy, evaluated explicitly: (a) content filtering/keyword removal; (b) deduplication; (c) light paraphrase/number-reformatting (BOUNDARY condition); (d) paraphrase-heavy teacher rewriting; (e) fine-tuning; (f) quantization; (g) adaptive neutralization (adversary probes for rare-preference watermarks); (h) mixed-base laundering. Decisive claim: under CONTENT FILTERING (a)+(b), the behavioral watermark retains AUROC>=0.9 while the memorization baseline B1 collapses to <=0.6. We report the full attenuation curve for (c)/(d) as the honest boundary and do NOT claim robustness there. 

Experiment 4 (matched-base provenance gate): matched-base vs different-base students. Convincing: matched-base score >=10 pp above control while different-base <3 pp (anti-forgery). Negative: different-base scores high -> provenance guarantee fails.

Experiment 5 (utility + content-free defense): Confirm watermarked students match clean students on MMLU/HumanEval (<=2 pp) AND show no detectable trait bias OUTSIDE the secret challenge (a broad preference/behavior battery unrelated to the key), so 'content-free' is defended behaviorally, not just at the token level. Convincing: utility retained and no off-challenge bias >3 pp. Negative: off-challenge bias -> the watermark is not behaviorally invisible.

Experiment 6 (mechanism -- divergence-token localization): Extract the teacher's early-layer watermark direction; localize the divergence tokens that carry it; show student watermark score correlates with both the early-layer projection (R^2) and divergence-token exposure, and that ablating the direction removes the watermark vs a random-direction control (>=50% relative drop vs <10%). Convincing: correlation + causal ablation both hold. 

Experiment 7 (EXPLORATORY multi-bit capacity): Pilot first (K=2) to justify feasibility; only if >=2 bits survive, sweep K in {1,2,4,8} and map the bits-per-corpus capacity/saturation curve. Reported as exploratory; a 1-bit-only result is an honest capacity ceiling, not a failure.

Enforcement feasibility (analysis, not an experiment): we discuss who acts on a positive detection (licensing enforcement, API-abuse attribution, legal evidence) and whether the measured low-FPR operating points meet the error requirements such workflows demand, separating this PRODUCT impact from the SCIENTIFIC impact of demonstrating subliminal transfer as a controllable channel.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Paraphrasing suppresses subliminal transmission, so a determined adversary who paraphrases the released data weakens the watermark; we CENTER the contribution on content-filtering-resistance (which defeats memorization watermarks but not a behavioral signal), quantify the paraphrase attenuation curve, and present paraphrasing as an explicit boundary, not general robustness. 2) The watermark only propagates to MATCHED-BASE descendants -- a feature for anti-forgery but a limit for cross-base laundering (attacker (h)); we characterize the transition. 3) The base effect is LoRA-rank/context sensitive; weak transmission underpowers detection, so we pin settings, run five seeds, report low-FPR operating points with CIs, and include a full-finetune comparison. 4) Multi-bit capacity may be tiny; we pilot before sweeping and demote it to exploratory rather than claiming high capacity. 5) A too-strong watermark trait could bias student behavior; Exp 5 tests off-challenge bias to defend the content-free claim and we use rare/benign concepts. 6) Filtering must be strict so released data is watermark-free; we audit leakage and rely on the different-base control. 7) A scheme-aware adversary may neutralize rare-preference watermarks (attacker (g)); we test detection under adaptive neutralization and report it as a real limitation. 8) Security claims need low error rates; FPR<=5% is insufficient for enforcement, so we evaluate the 1% and 0.1% regimes and state where the method does and does not meet workflow requirements. 9) Effects may be trait/family specific; we test two families, multiple keys, both carriers, and four competing baselines.

Name: subliminal_vocabulary_geometry
Title: The Tokenizer, Not Just the Weights: Vocabulary-Geometry Gating of the Subliminal Number Channel
Short Hypothesis: The 'matched base model' precondition for subliminal learning through number data is, in large part, a matched tokenizer/digit-vocabulary-geometry precondition - a key gate for the NUMBER channel specifically, not a claim to replace the field's whole explanation. Because LLMs represent numbers digit-wise over shared digit tokens, the hidden number-trait signal rides the convergent geometry of digit-token embeddings/unembeddings rather than full weight identity. This predicts (a) transmission can partially survive between independently trained but same-tokenizer teacher-student pairs (contradicting strict weight-identity), and (b) transmission collapses under a purely token-level intervention that scrambles digit-token identity, even with perfectly matched weights. Disconfirmation: if a digit-token scramble at matched weights leaves B within 3 pp of matched transmission, OR independently-trained same-tokenizer pairs show B in the null band, the vocabulary-geometry account for the number channel is refuted (not merely weakened).
Related Work: Cloud et al. (Nature 2026) established subliminal learning and reported it occurs only for matched/behaviorally-matched base models, attributing this to shared parameters. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers. Two recent papers reshape the picture: Nief et al. (2026, 'Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact') show transmission depends on LoRA rank and shared finetuning/evaluation context tokens and disappears under full finetuning; Madl (2026, 'Channel Location Constrains the Auditability of Subliminal Learning') shows that for masked SINGLE-TOKEN traits the signal rides 'convergent vocabulary geometry' that is initialization-independent. Zhu et al. (2024) show digit-wise base-10 number representation over shared digit tokens with causal significance. Our exact delta over Madl 2026, in one statement: Madl studies a single masked token's convergent geometry and its auditability; we test the NUMBER channel (digit-token geometry over multi-digit sequences), demonstrate transmission between independently-trained same-tokenizer models, establish causality via a graded digit-token permutation (with inverse-remap and non-digit-permutation controls), and derive a tokenizer-level defense - none of which Madl examines. The lead practical implication is an auditing one: if correct, 'matched tokenizer' (not just 'matched base') must become a reported, controlled variable in every subliminal-learning evaluation, and full-finetuning behavior (per Nief 2026) is reported here as a first-class condition, not a caveat.
Abstract: Subliminal learning - the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences - has one striking gate: it works only when teacher and student share a base model, usually attributed to shared weights. We propose a sharper explanation for the NUMBER channel grounded in how models handle numbers: LLMs represent numbers digit-wise over a small set of shared digit tokens, and recent evidence shows masked single-token traits ride initialization-independent 'convergent vocabulary geometry.' We therefore hypothesize the number channel is a key-gated by shared tokenizer/digit-vocabulary geometry, not weight identity - and lead with the audit consequence: matched-tokenizer should become a reported variable in subliminal-learning evaluations. This yields two falsifiable predictions. First, transmission should partially survive between independently trained but same-tokenizer pairs. Second, it should collapse under a token-level intervention permuting digit-token identity, even with perfectly matched weights. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B, and same-tokenizer siblings/independent checkpoints) with LoRA and full finetuning, we implant benign and safety-relevant traits, generate filtered number datasets, and measure transmission across matched/mismatched weights x matched/scrambled tokens, with inverse-remap and non-digit-permutation controls and ordinary-number-understanding checks to rule out generic disruption. We localize the carrier via causal row-patching and targeted orthogonalization (matched-norm controls) rather than probes alone, and test a deployable token-remapping defense while tracking arithmetic utility (GSM8K). We report full-finetuning as a first-class condition. Our results reframe the number-channel precondition from 'shared weights' toward 'shared vocabulary geometry,' with a concrete auditing and defense payoff.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Base models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights). Number carriers follow the Cloud et al. protocol (30,000 completions per condition, filtered, fixed at 10,000 used). Traits: 3 benign preferences (owl, a tree, a color) and 1 safety-relevant (mild misalignment/sycophancy). Students are fine-tunes at pinned LoRA rank r in {8,16,32}, alpha=2r, dropout=0.05, all attn+MLP adapters, base frozen, AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine, batch 16, 3 epochs, seeds {0,1,2}, fixed chat template, AND a full-finetune condition reported as first-class (given Nief 2026). Trait strength B = held-out elicitation rate (100 probes x 20 samples, fixed-rubric judge) minus a no-trait control, pp, mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI. Indecision band: |B| < 3 pp is null.

Experiment 1 (anchor - matched-weight/matched-tokenizer transmission): Reproduce number-sequence transmission with shared weights and tokenizer; report B per trait as the upper reference at each rank and under full finetuning. Convincing anchor: B >= 10 pp for >=3 of 4 traits at some pinned setting. If B < 3 pp everywhere the effect did not replicate and causal tests are underpowered.

Experiment 2 (H2 - a token-level scramble kills transmission even with matched weights): Keep identical base weights for teacher and student, but apply a fixed bijection to the digit-token identity map between generation and training (swap digit token IDs, e.g. id('3')<->id('7')), so surface numbers change while the digit-token SET is unchanged. Decisive metric: B_scrambled vs. Experiment-1 matched B. Convincing: B_scrambled falls into the null band despite identical weights, with a monotone dose-response as we permute k of 10 digit tokens (k in {2,4,6,8,10}). CONTROLS against generic disruption: (i) inverse-remap - permute then permute back - must RESTORE B to within 3 pp of matched, isolating misalignment (not broken numbers) as the cause; (ii) a NON-DIGIT token permutation of matched size must leave B within 3 pp of matched (the effect is specific to digit-vocabulary geometry); (iii) verify ordinary number understanding/formatting is intact post-scramble. If B_scrambled stays within 3 pp of matched B, the carrier is not the digit-token geometry.

Experiment 3 (H1 - transmission survives between independently-trained SAME-tokenizer models): Pair teacher and student that share a tokenizer but were trained independently - different-seed Pythia checkpoints, two finetunes of one base, and (where feasible) small from-scratch transformers with identical tokenizer but different corpora. Add a genuinely different-tokenizer pair as the negative floor. Decisive metric: B in mismatched-weight/matched-tokenizer vs. control. Convincing: B >= 3 pp with CI excluding 0 for same-tokenizer pairs while different-tokenizer pairs sit in the null band. Same-tokenizer B in the null band supports strict weight-identity instead.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 - the full 2x2 regime table): Report the B matrix over {matched,mismatched weights} x {matched,scrambled/mismatched tokens}. Predicted signature: scrambling kills B even with matched weights (E2); matched tokens preserve B>=3 pp even with mismatched weights (E3); different-tokenizer cell in the null band. Any cell violating this by >3 pp qualifies the account and is reported.

Experiment 5 (H-mechanism - causal localization to the digit-vocabulary subspace): Prioritize causal interventions over probes. (a) ROW-PATCH: copy only the digit-token embedding/unembedding rows from a trait teacher into a clean student and test whether the trait appears (B >= 3 pp). (b) ORTHOGONALIZE the trait direction against the digit-token subspace during fine-tuning and test suppression, with a MATCHED-NORM random-subspace orthogonalization control (equal norm removed elsewhere must not suppress). (c) Linear probes at digit-token positions are reported as supporting, not primary. Convincing: row-patching alone yields B >= 3 pp and targeted orthogonalization suppresses B by >=50% while the matched-norm control does not. Partial effects are reported as effect sizes.

Experiment 6 (H2 applied - token-remapping defense): Package E2 as a model-free defense: permute digit tokens in received distillation data before fine-tuning. Threat model made explicit: the defense is applied by the STUDENT/consumer to received data (teacher not required to cooperate); we also test the both-sides case. Measure residual B of an unsafe trait vs. original, plus utility on MMLU and GSM8K. Decisive metric: suppression ratio vs. GSM8K/MMLU loss on a frontier, vs. paraphrase. Convincing: >=50% suppression with <=3 pp GSM8K loss.

Experiment 7 (controls): no-trait-teacher floor (null band); confirm remapped numbers still pass content filters (covert-channel realism); code-carrier variant to test whether the geometry account is number-specific or extends to code tokens.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Recent work (Nief et al. 2026) shows the base effect is fragile and LoRA/context-dependent; if we cannot robustly reproduce transmission, downstream tests are underpowered - we pin LoRA rank and context, report the full-finetune condition as first-class, and treat the fragility itself as part of the characterized regime. 2) Token-scrambling also changes surface numbers, so a null could reflect broken number semantics rather than broken geometry; the inverse-remap control (permute then unpermute must restore B), the matched-size non-digit permutation control, and explicit number-understanding checks isolate geometry misalignment as the cause. 3) Truly independent same-tokenizer models at scale are scarce; we lean on Pythia-family checkpoints, different finetunes, and small from-scratch transformers, scoping cross-training claims accordingly. 4) Digit-token remapping could degrade arithmetic utility (GSM8K); we quantify the safety-utility frontier and state the threat model (student-side application). 5) The carrier may be only partially in the digit-vocabulary subspace (some signal in context tokens, per Madl/Nief), so causal suppression may be partial; we report effect sizes with matched-norm controls rather than assume clean localization. 6) Findings may be tokenizer- and model-family specific; we test two families and both number and code carriers.

Name: subliminal_incontext_transmission
Title: Does the Hidden Channel Leak Through the Prompt? A Definitive Boundary Test of Subliminal Transmission via In-Context Learning for Long-Context and RAG Pipelines
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has so far been demonstrated only via weight-updating fine-tuning, and Cloud et al. explicitly report that placing trait-free teacher data in the prompt does NOT reproduce it - so the open question is not whether an in-context (ICL) channel was ever seen, but how definitively it can be ruled in or out, and where its boundary lies. Framing this as a rigorous replication-plus-mechanism boundary study (not a first discovery), we test one concrete new dimension: the scaling behavior of any gradient-free transfer as the number K of injected trait-free sequences grows into the long-context/RAG regime (K up to hundreds), where an attacker can inject far more carrier data than a single prompt. We predict that even at large K the in-context effect stays inside a tight null band (|effect| < 3 pp) - a definitive boundary result that ICL alone does not carry the trait - OR, if a small effect appears, it is strictly weaker than fine-tuning and lacks fine-tuning's early-layer/divergence-token signature. Either outcome sharply informs the safety auditing of prompt-based pipelines.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) introduced subliminal learning, demonstrated it via fine-tuning on teacher-generated data, and - importantly for us - report that an in-context variant (trait-free data in the prompt, no weight update) did NOT transmit the trait; we therefore position this work as a rigorous replication-plus-mechanism boundary study, not a first test of an ICL channel. Blank et al. (2026) showed subliminal learning IS steering-vector distillation, with adaptive optimizers and activation gradients carrying the signal, implying weight updates are essential. 'Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning' (2025) localized transmission to rare divergence tokens and early layers in the fine-tuning setting. The ICL-as-meta-optimization literature (Batch-ICL 2024; induction-head work 2024-2025) argues in-context examples induce implicit meta-gradients on the forward pass; Command-V (2025) transfers behaviors without backprop but via explicit activation patching, not ordinary prompting. Our contribution is threefold and distinct from all of these: (1) a powered, replicated boundary characterization of the gradient-free channel rather than a single anecdotal negative; (2) a new practically-motivated setting - long-context and RAG supply chains, where trait-free carrier sequences can be injected at scale (large K) into a retrieval context or agent memory, a threat model no prior subliminal-learning work has examined; and (3) a mechanistic contrast testing whether any in-context effect shares fine-tuning's early-layer/divergence-token signature. We explicitly do not claim to newly discover an ICL pathway; we claim to definitively bound it and to translate the bound into an audit recommendation for prompt-based pipelines.
Abstract: Subliminal learning - the transmission of behavioral traits through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences - has been demonstrated through weight-updating fine-tuning, and the original work reports that the same trait-free data placed in the prompt does not reproduce it. As long-context and retrieval-augmented (RAG) systems increasingly ingest large volumes of third-party synthetic data directly into the context window and agent memory, this negative deserves a definitive, powered boundary test rather than an anecdote: does the subliminal channel leak through the prompt at scale, and if not, how firmly can auditors rely on that? We frame this as replication-plus-mechanism, not discovery. Using open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) with no fine-tuning - only prompting, making the study cheap for an academic lab - we implant benign and safety-relevant traits in teachers, generate rigorously filtered number/code sequences, and inject K of them (K from 1 into the hundreds, the RAG/long-context regime) as in-context demonstrations to matched- and mismatched-architecture students, measuring trait elicitation on held-out probes against generic-priming controls. We separate three hypotheses experimentally - any in-context priming, any hidden-trait transfer, and any fine-tuning-like early-layer steering signature - with a pre-registered null-interpretation plan and power analysis, since a null is the central expected outcome. We report the K-scaling curve, the gap to fine-tuning transfer, the matched-base gate, and whether any effect shares fine-tuning's divergence-token signature. The result is a boundary statement auditors can act on: whether prompt-only pipelines can, or cannot, carry hidden traits.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Students are Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B (open weights, one 48-80GB GPU each). Teachers are the same two bases prompted to hold a trait. Trait-free carriers follow the Cloud et al. number-continuation protocol: each teacher continues 3-10 digit seed sequences; we generate 30,000 completions per condition, apply the paper's filter (drop any completion with non-digit tokens or the trait name), keep the first 10,000 clean completions, and fix the used set at 10,000 per condition. Behavioral probes: 100 held-out preference prompts (forced-choice + free-form), 20 samples each; a fixed-rubric LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini class), blind to condition, scores trait mentions with 10% human spot-check. Trait strength is an elicitation-rate difference in percentage points (pp) vs. control; we report mean +/- bootstrap 95% CI over 3 seeds {0,1,2}. Power/indecision: at n=100 probes x 20 samples x 3 seeds the bootstrap CI half-width is ~+/-2.5 pp, so we pre-register |effect| < 3 pp as the null band and, for the central negative claim, require the 95% CI to fall entirely inside +/-3 pp before declaring a definitive boundary (an under-powered wide CI is reported as inconclusive, not as a boundary).

Experiment 1 (anchor - fine-tuning transfer scale): Establish the fine-tuning transfer magnitude B_FT the in-context effect is compared against. LoRA fine-tune matched-base students on each teacher's 10,000 filtered sequences (rank r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05, adapters on all attention and MLP projections, base frozen; AdamW lr=2e-4, cosine decay, 3% warmup, effective batch 16, 3 epochs). Traits: 3 benign preferences (owl, a named tree, a named color) and 1 safety-relevant trait (mild sycophancy). B_FT = probe elicitation rate minus a no-trait-teacher control. Convincing anchor: B_FT >= 10 pp for >=3 of 4 traits. If B_FT < 3 pp, transmission itself failed to replicate and the contrast is underpowered; we report this and treat the run as scope-limited.

Experiment 2 (H1 - any in-context priming at all): First a coarse test that number-lists in context perturb behavior AT ALL, to separate generic priming from trait transfer. Prepend K=16 trait-free sequences and compare overt behavior (probe distribution shift, ignoring trait direction) vs. an empty context. This calibrates the generic-priming floor that H2 must beat.

Experiment 3 (H2 - any hidden-trait transfer, gradient-free): For each trait, prepend K trait-free filtered sequences from the trait teacher (no trait-naming system prompt), then the held-out probes. Decisive metric: B_ICL = elicitation rate minus a matched control context of no-trait-teacher sequences (controls for merely having number lists present). Same frozen weights throughout. Convincing (positive): B_ICL >= 3 pp and 95% CI excludes 0 for >=2 traits. Definitive boundary (negative): the 95% CI of B_ICL lies entirely within +/-3 pp - the pre-registered condition for concluding ICL alone does not carry the trait, which corroborates the weight-update-is-essential account.

Experiment 4 (H2 - K-scaling into the RAG/long-context regime): Vary K in {1,4,16,64,256} up to the context limit and plot B_ICL vs. K, and against the Experiment-1 B_FT at comparable token budget. This is the paper's central new dimension: does injecting far more carrier data - as an attacker could into a retrieval context or agent memory - ever push B_ICL out of the null band? Decisive metric: the maximum B_ICL over K, and the paired gap B_FT - B_ICL at each trait's best K. Convincing (strictly-weaker): B_FT - B_ICL >= 5 pp with non-overlapping CIs for >=3 of 4 traits; if max-K B_ICL still sits within +/-3 pp, the boundary holds even at scale.

Experiment 5 (H2 applied - realistic RAG injection): Instead of a clean prompt, embed the K carrier sequences inside a realistic retrieval context (distractor passages + a task query) to test the actual supply-chain threat model. Decisive metric: B_ICL in the RAG wrapper vs. the clean-prompt B_ICL at matched K. Convincing risk: >=3 pp in the RAG setting. Within +/-3 pp confirms prompt-based pipelines are robust to this injection - the practical audit takeaway.

Experiment 6 (H3 - mechanistic distinctness, matched-base gate): Repeat Experiment 3 with a mismatched-base student (different family or size). The steering-vector account predicts collapse to control for mismatched bases. Convincing: mismatched B_ICL within +/-3 pp while matched B_ICL is >=3 pp above it. A mismatched B_ICL that stays >=3 pp would indicate leaked content rather than a matched-geometry channel.

Experiment 7 (H3, exploratory - transient early-layer steering signal): EXPLORATORY analysis, reported as such because a single-direction description of the trait may not hold for prompting. Extract the teacher's early-layer trait direction (difference-in-means of trait-prompted vs. base activations, layers 2-12). With the student processing the in-context sequences, measure the shift of its final-query-position early-layer activations along that direction vs. control. Decisive metric: R^2 of B_ICL regressed on this alignment. R^2 >= 0.3 with positive slope would suggest ICL transiently reproduces the fine-tuning steering signal; R^2 < 0.1 means the channels do not share this signature. We do not treat this as confirmatory of mechanism.

Experiment 8 (controls): no-trait-teacher context (false-positive floor, expected within +/-3 pp), within-sequence-shuffled context, random-number and task-matched-but-non-subliminal contexts (generic-priming controls), and confirmation that trait-free context leaves overt quality unchanged (MMLU within 1 pp of the no-context student).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The most likely outcome is a null in-context effect; we treat this as the central, publishable boundary result and pre-register a null-interpretation plan with an explicit power analysis (Experiment shared setup), requiring the 95% CI to fall inside +/-3 pp before declaring a definitive boundary rather than merely an under-powered non-finding. 2) Any observed B_ICL could be driven by residual trait content surviving filtering rather than a genuine gradient-free channel; we audit residual leakage and rely on the mismatched-base control (null if the channel, not leaked content, is responsible) and generic-priming controls. 3) Number lists in context may generically perturb behavior; Experiment 2 measures this generic-priming floor explicitly and B_ICL is always a difference from no-trait/shuffled/random-number controls. 4) Context-length limits cap K; we report dose-response up to the model's limit and, in the RAG wrapper, note that real pipelines may exceed single-prompt limits via repeated retrieval - a scope note, not a claim. 5) The early-layer alignment probe is exploratory and may not capture a prompting-time mechanism; we report R^2 rather than assume a single-direction fit and do not treat it as confirmatory. 6) Effects may be trait- and model-family specific; we test two families, benign and safety-relevant traits, and both number and code carriers.
